disease.name: Gastritis
disease.icd_10_code: K29.0 (Acute haemorrhagic gastritis); K29.1 (Other acute gastritis); K29.2 (Alcoholic gastritis); K29.3 (Chronic superficial gastritis); K29.4 (Chronic atrophic gastritis); K29.5 (Unspecified chronic gastritis); K29.6 (Other gastritis — including granulomatous, eosinophilic); K29.7 (Gastritis, unspecified); K29.8 (Duodenitis); B96.81 (H. pylori as cause of disease classified elsewhere — used with K29); K31.9 (Disease of stomach and duodenum, unspecified)
disease.category: Gastroenterology / Upper Gastrointestinal Disease / Mucosal Disease

overview.description: Gastritis is a broad clinical and pathological term denoting inflammatory change in the gastric mucosa — the specialised inner lining of the stomach responsible for producing hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen, intrinsic factor, and mucus. Inflammation can range from a transient superficial mucosal redness (acute gastritis) to progressive destruction of gastric glands with permanent loss of acid-secreting parietal cells and pepsin-secreting chief cells (chronic atrophic gastritis). An important and frequently misunderstood distinction: GASTRITIS is a histopathological and endoscopic diagnosis — it refers to actual mucosal inflammation confirmed by biopsy or endoscopy; whereas DYSPEPSIA is a symptom complex (epigastric pain, nausea, bloating) that often does not correlate with underlying mucosal inflammation. Many patients with histologically confirmed gastritis have NO symptoms, while many patients with severe dyspeptic symptoms have a normal gastric mucosa. This dissociation between pathology and symptoms is one of the defining challenges of gastritis management. Helicobacter pylori infection is the single most important cause of gastritis globally — responsible for approximately 90% of chronic gastritis and the primary driver of the Correa cascade (the stepwise progression from H. pylori gastritis → chronic atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → gastric adenocarcinoma), the most significant carcinogenic pathway in the stomach. In India, with an H. pylori prevalence of 70-80%, gastritis is extraordinarily common — though the vast majority of cases remain asymptomatic and undiagnosed. The treatment paradigm has shifted from symptom management to disease modification: H. pylori eradication halts progression along the cancer cascade, reduces peptic ulcer disease, and may allow partial mucosal regeneration even in atrophic gastritis.
overview.affected_organ: Gastric mucosa (antrum, corpus/body, fundus, cardia) — affecting gastric parietal cells (acid secretion), chief cells (pepsinogen), mucous neck cells (mucus), and enteroendocrine cells (gastrin — G cells; somatostatin — D cells; histamine — ECL cells)
overview.prevalence: Gastritis is one of the most prevalent conditions globally; H. pylori gastritis (the dominant form) affects approximately 50% of the world population; in India: 70-80% of adults are infected with H. pylori making gastritis virtually ubiquitous; atrophic gastritis affects approximately 5-10% of the adult Indian population; autoimmune gastritis affects 2-5% of elderly individuals (more common in women and in populations of Northern European descent)
overview.age_group: Acute gastritis: all ages; Chronic H. pylori gastritis: acquired in childhood (most Indian adults infected by age 10); progressive throughout adult life; Autoimmune gastritis: predominantly women over 40 years; Stress gastritis: critically ill patients in ICU; NSAID-induced gastritis: increasing with age (higher NSAID use in elderly)
overview.is_contagious_note: Gastritis itself is not contagious; H. pylori — the causative agent of most gastritis — is transmissible via fecal-oral and oral-oral routes and may spread within households
overview.is_curable_note: H. pylori gastritis is CURABLE with successful H. pylori eradication — inflammation resolves completely in most cases after eradication; atrophic gastritis may partially reverse after H. pylori eradication in early stages but advanced atrophy with intestinal metaplasia is largely irreversible. Autoimmune gastritis is not curable — treatment addresses consequences (B12 replacement) and monitors for cancer. NSAID/alcohol-induced gastritis is fully reversible with cessation of causative agent.
overview.is_chronic_note: Acute gastritis resolves within days to weeks; chronic gastritis (H. pylori, autoimmune, chemical) persists indefinitely without treatment intervention
overview.key_fact: Gastritis from H. pylori is the single most important preventable and treatable cause of stomach cancer globally — responsible for 89% of non-cardia gastric cancers. A simple urea breath test and a 10-14 day antibiotic course can eradicate H. pylori, halt gastric carcinogenesis, and potentially prevent stomach cancer. Every Indian adult with dyspepsia, gastric ulcer, or unexplained iron deficiency should be tested and treated for H. pylori.

types.name: Acute Gastritis
types.description: Acute onset gastric mucosal inflammation characterised by neutrophilic infiltration (polymorphonuclear leucocytes in the mucosal epithelium and lamina propria). Unlike chronic gastritis, acute gastritis is typically symptomatic, often self-limiting, and resolves completely when the causative agent is removed. Endoscopically characterised by mucosal oedema, erythema, erosions, or haemorrhage depending on aetiology and severity.

subtypes.description: The initial gastric mucosal response to primary H. pylori infection — a self-limiting acute gastritis that occurs at the time of first H. pylori acquisition (typically childhood in India). Characterised by: transient symptomatic illness (nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, halitosis); hypochlorhydria (temporary acid reduction from mucosal inflammation); neutrophilic infiltration of the antrum and sometimes corpus. After this acute phase, approximately 80% of infected individuals develop chronic active gastritis that persists lifelong without treatment. Most initial H. pylori acquisition is completely asymptomatic.
subtypes.resolution: The acute symptomatic phase lasts 1-2 weeks and resolves spontaneously; however, H. pylori colonisation persists indefinitely without eradication therapy, converting to chronic gastritis

subtypes.description: Mucosal damage characterised by multiple superficial erosions (epithelial defects not extending through the muscularis mucosae — distinguishing them from ulcers) with or without haemorrhage. Common causes include alcohol, NSAIDs, and severe physiological stress (see stress gastritis). May present with haematemesis (vomiting blood) or melaena (black stools) from superficial mucosal bleeding.
subtypes.causes: Alcohol (direct mucosal cytotoxicity; increases mucosal permeability); NSAIDs (prostaglandin synthesis inhibition depleting mucosal defence); aspirin; concentrated chemical ingestion; bile reflux; cocaine use
subtypes.management: Remove causative agent; PPIs (IV pantoprazole for haemorrhage); antacids; sucralfate; generally heals rapidly (days to weeks) once cause removed

subtypes.subtype: Acute Stress Gastritis (Stress Ulcers / Stress-Related Mucosal Disease — SRMD)
subtypes.description: Acute mucosal injury developing in critically ill patients admitted to the intensive care unit — characterised by multiple superficial erosions throughout the gastric fundus and body, sometimes extending to the duodenum. SRMD affects up to 75-100% of ICU patients histologically, though clinically significant bleeding occurs in 2-6% (without prophylaxis). Life-threatening bleeding from stress ulcers occurs in 0.5-1.5% of ICU patients.
subtypes.pathogenesis: Critical illness (sepsis, major trauma, mechanical ventilation, burns, head injury, hepatic or renal failure, major surgery) causes: mucosal ischaemia from reduced splanchnic blood flow; impaired mucosal regeneration; increased acid back-diffusion; reduced prostaglandin synthesis — all breaching the normally protective gastric mucosal barrier
subtypes.risk_factors: Mechanical ventilation >48 hours (most important); coagulopathy (platelet <50,000 or INR >1.5); severe sepsis and septic shock; head injury with GCS <10 or intracranial hypertension; major burns (>35% BSA — Curling's ulcer); hepatic failure; renal failure; high-dose corticosteroids
subtypes.diagnosis: Endoscopy — multiple shallow erosions predominantly in fundus and body (proximal stomach); differs from H. pylori gastritis (predominantly antral)
subtypes.prevention: STRESS ULCER PROPHYLAXIS — IV pantoprazole 40 mg once or twice daily or oral PPI when GI tract accessible; IV H2 blockers (famotidine) as alternative; ONLY in high-risk ICU patients (mechanical ventilation >48h; coagulopathy); do NOT give prophylaxis to all hospitalised patients (increases C. difficile and pneumonia risk); ENTERAL NUTRITION started early is as effective as PPI prophylaxis for low-risk ICU patients

types.name: Chronic H. pylori Gastritis (Type B Gastritis — Antral Gastritis)
types.description: The most common form of chronic gastritis worldwide — affecting approximately 50% of the world's population and 70-80% of India. Caused by persistent H. pylori colonisation of the gastric mucosa establishing a chronic active gastritis characterised by: a mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages — chronic component; neutrophils — active component); lymphoid follicle formation (creating 'lymphoid follicular gastritis' — the precursor lesion for gastric MALT lymphoma); progressive progression from antral-predominant inflammation toward body involvement over decades. H. pylori gastritis is the essential starting point of the Correa carcinogenesis cascade — the stepwise progression from normal mucosa to gastric cancer.
types.topographic_distribution: Initially antrum-predominant (most H. pylori strains colonise preferentially in the antrum where pH is higher); progresses proximally to involve the corpus/body over years to decades; some CagA-positive strains cause pangastritis (both antrum and body) — associated with higher atrophy and cancer risk; corpus-predominant H. pylori gastritis leads to more profound acid suppression (atrophy of acid-secreting parietal cells in the body)

the_correa_cascade.description: The stepwise pathological progression from H. pylori infection to invasive gastric adenocarcinoma — the most important paradigm in gastric oncology.
steps: Step 2: H. pylori chronic active gastritis (H. pylori colonisation triggers chronic neutrophilic and mononuclear inflammation)
Step 3: Chronic atrophic gastritis (progressive loss of normal gastric glands — parietal cells and chief cells — replaced by fibrous tissue)

Step 4: Intestinal metaplasia (replacement of gastric epithelium with intestinal-type epithelium — goblet cells appear; complete [Type I] and incomplete [Type II/III] subtypes; incomplete intestinal metaplasia carries higher cancer risk)
Step 5: Dysplasia (low-grade then high-grade — nuclear atypia, gland abnormalities; precancerous lesion)
Step 6: Invasive gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal type — the most common H. pylori-associated gastric cancer)
the_correa_cascade.risk_factors_for_progression: CagA-positive H. pylori strains; VacA s1m1 genotype; high salt diet; smoking; alcohol; low fruit and vegetable intake; family history of gastric cancer; blood group A (higher cancer risk); genetic polymorphisms (IL-1B, TNF-alpha, IL-10); chronic NSAID use may paradoxically be mildly protective against cancer progression (anti-inflammatory effect)
the_correa_cascade.reversibility: Steps 1-3 are largely reversible with H. pylori eradication; Step 4 (intestinal metaplasia) is partially reversible in early stages; Steps 5-6 are not reversed by eradication — require endoscopic or surgical management; H. pylori eradication at any stage reduces the risk of progression and reduces gastric cancer incidence by approximately 50%

sydney_classification.description: The Updated Sydney Classification System (1996) provides a standardised histological framework for grading gastritis. Based on endoscopic mapping with systematic biopsies from five sites (antrum greater curvature, antrum lesser curvature, incisura angularis, corpus greater curvature, corpus lesser curvature) and assessment of five variables on a four-point scale (0=none, 1=mild, 2=moderate, 3=severe):

olga_staging.description: OLGA (Operative Link for Gastritis Assessment) and OLGIM (for Intestinal Metaplasia) are histopathological staging systems combining the extent (antrum vs corpus) and severity of atrophy or intestinal metaplasia to stratify cancer risk and guide surveillance intervals.
stages: OLGA Stage 0: No atrophy in antrum or corpus — LOW RISK; surveillance optional/low priority
OLGA Stage I: Mild atrophy in antrum, none in corpus — LOW RISK
OLGA Stage II: Moderate/severe atrophy in antrum or mild in corpus — INTERMEDIATE RISK
OLGA Stage III: Severe antral atrophy OR moderate corpus atrophy — HIGH RISK — endoscopic surveillance every 3 years
OLGA Stage IV: Severe atrophy in both antrum and corpus — HIGHEST RISK — endoscopic surveillance every 3 years
olga_staging.surveillance_recommendation: OLGA/OLGIM Stage III-IV: endoscopic surveillance every 3 years (BSG 2019, ESGE 2019 guidelines); H. pylori eradication at all stages reduces progression risk; Vitamin C and antioxidant supplementation may slow progression (limited evidence)

types.name: Autoimmune Gastritis (Type A Gastritis — Corporal Atrophic Gastritis / Pernicious Anaemia Gastritis)
types.description: A progressive autoimmune destruction of the gastric body and fundus mucosa — specifically targeting the acid-secreting parietal cells and their product intrinsic factor. Autoimmune gastritis accounts for approximately 5-10% of all chronic gastritis and is the primary cause of pernicious anaemia. It is characterised by: CORPUS-PREDOMINANT atrophy (unlike H. pylori gastritis which begins in the antrum); virtually NO antral involvement (the antrum is spared — opposite pattern to H. pylori); detectable circulating autoantibodies; profound hypochlorhydria to achlorhydria (no acid production); extreme hypergastrinaemia (gastrin levels may be 10-100× normal — loss of acid removes the negative feedback loop on G cells in the preserved antrum); and ECL-cell hyperplasia progressing to type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumours (carcinoids).
types.pathogenesis: CD4+ T-lymphocyte-mediated autoimmune attack on gastric parietal cells; anti-parietal cell antibodies (APCA) — directed against H+/K+-ATPase (the proton pump); anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (anti-IF) — type 1 (blocking antibody — prevents B12 binding to IF); type 2 (binding antibody — prevents IF-B12 complex from binding to ileal receptor); LOSS OF PARIETAL CELLS → achlorhydria → loss of negative acid feedback → G-cell hyperplasia → hypergastrinaemia → prolonged gastrin stimulation of ECL cells → ECL hyperplasia → dysplasia → type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumours
key_features: CORPUS-PREDOMINANT (body and fundus) atrophic gastritis — ANTRUM SPARED
Achlorhydria (no gastric acid — gastric pH permanently >4-5)
Markedly elevated serum gastrin (compensatory — from G cells in antrum not inhibited by acid)
Positive anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (Type 1 or 2) in 50-70%
Pernicious anaemia — B12 deficiency from absent intrinsic factor (IF is exclusively from parietal cells)
Iron deficiency anaemia — achlorhydria impairs iron absorption (requires acid for ferric to ferrous conversion)
Risk of GASTRIC CANCER (1% per year) and TYPE 1 GASTRIC NEUROENDOCRINE TUMOURS (multiple small carcinoids in ECL hyperplasia)
associated_conditions: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus — autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type III
Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease)
types.diagnosis_specific: Anti-parietal cell antibodies (APCA): 90% sensitivity but low specificity (present in 10% of healthy adults); Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (type 1 blocking Ab): 50-70% sensitivity but HIGH SPECIFICITY (>95%) for autoimmune gastritis — highly specific when positive; Serum gastrin: markedly elevated (>200 pg/mL — often >500-1000); Serum pepsinogen I: very low (parietal cells and chief cells both lost); Pepsinogen I/II ratio: <3 (suggests severe corpus atrophy); Vitamin B12: low; Methylmalonic acid (MMA) and homocysteine: elevated (sensitive markers of functional B12 deficiency even before overt anaemia)
types.type_1_gastric_neuroendocrine_tumours: ECL-cell neuroendocrine tumours (carcinoids) arising in the setting of autoimmune gastritis and hypergastrinaemia; typically small (<1 cm), multiple, and in the gastric body/fundus; low-grade malignancy; indolent behaviour; most do not metastasise; treat by endoscopic resection if >1 cm; antrectomy reduces gastrin drive and may cause regression of small carcinoids

types.name: Chemical / Reactive Gastritis (Type C Gastritis)
types.description: Gastric mucosal injury from CHEMICAL IRRITANTS — primarily bile reflux from the duodenum into the stomach (most common after partial gastrectomy or pyloroplasty), or NSAIDs/aspirin-induced direct mucosal injury. Unlike H. pylori gastritis, chemical gastropathy is characterised histologically by: foveolar hyperplasia (elongated, tortuous gastric pits); oedema and smooth muscle proliferation in the lamina propria; minimal or absent inflammatory infiltrate (it is a REACTIVE change, not a true inflammatory infiltrate — hence 'gastropathy' rather than 'gastritis' in strict terminology); and vascular congestion.
causes: Bile reflux gastropathy: most common after Billroth II gastrectomy, pyloroplasty, or gastrojejunostomy; also in intact stomach (bile reflux without surgery — duodenogastric reflux); bile acids are directly cytotoxic to gastric epithelium
NSAID gastropathy: direct topical irritation; inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis (depletes mucosal defence); typically involves antrum and prepyloric region; may cause erosions and ulcers
Aspirin: same mechanism as NSAIDs; even low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg/day) causes gastric mucosal injury
Alcohol: direct mucosal cytotoxicity; increases mucosal permeability; causes acute erosive gastritis acutely; chronic alcohol use → chronic reactive changes
types.diagnosis: Endoscopy with biopsy: foveolar hyperplasia + minimal inflammation + smooth muscle fibres in lamina propria = reactive gastropathy (characteristic Sydney system pattern); bile in stomach on endoscopy; bile pool visible at gastroscopy
types.management: Remove causative agent; bile reflux: sucralfate (coats mucosa); cholestyramine (binds bile); ursodeoxycholic acid; prokinetics to improve gastric emptying; surgical revision if severe; NSAID-induced: PPI co-prescription; switch to COX-2 inhibitor; replace NSAIDs with paracetamol where possible

types.name: Eosinophilic Gastritis
types.description: A rare inflammatory condition characterised by dense eosinophilic infiltration of the gastric wall (>30 eosinophils per high-power field in multiple biopsies) in the absence of secondary causes of gastric eosinophilia (parasitic infection, H. pylori, IBD, drug reactions, systemic hypereosinophilic syndrome). Part of the spectrum of eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders (EGIDs) which also includes eosinophilic oesophagitis (EoE) and eosinophilic enteritis. Often associated with atopy (food allergy, asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis).
types.clinical_features: Epigastric pain; nausea and vomiting; early satiety; weight loss; peripheral blood eosinophilia (in 70-80%); elevated serum IgE; protein-losing enteropathy (hypoalbuminaemia from mucosal loss of protein); ascites; oedema
types.diagnosis: Endoscopy: may appear normal or show nodularity, oedema, ulceration; biopsy (multiple biopsies from all stomach regions — eosinophilic infiltration is patchy); serum IgE; food allergy testing; peripheral blood count (eosinophilia); exclude parasites (stool OCP); allergy evaluation
types.management: Food elimination diet (remove common allergens: milk, wheat, soy, egg, nuts, seafood — 6-food elimination diet); oral corticosteroids (first-line when dietary restriction fails — prednisolone 20-40 mg/day); budesonide (targeted steroid); proton pump inhibitor (adjunct — some improvement); montelukast; mepolizumab (anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibody — for refractory eosinophilic GI disorders; evidence emerging)

types.name: Granulomatous Gastritis
types.description: Gastritis characterised by granuloma formation (aggregates of epithelioid histiocytes, often with Langhans giant cells) in the gastric wall. Rare — constitutes <1% of gastritis. Requires exclusion of specific infectious causes particularly important in India.
causes: Crohn's disease — most common cause of granulomatous gastritis in Western countries; gastric involvement occurs in 10-20% of Crohn's patients (upper GI Crohn's)
Sarcoidosis — systemic granulomatous disease; gastric sarcoid involvement is rare (0.5%) but well-documented
Mycobacterium tuberculosis — IMPORTANT IN INDIA — gastric TB is rare but can cause granulomatous gastritis; usually haematogenous spread; must rule out TB in India whenever gastric granulomas found
Idiopathic (isolated granulomatous gastritis) — diagnosis of exclusion
types.diagnosis: Endoscopy with biopsy; Ziehl-Neelsen stain for AFB; culture for Mycobacterium; special stains for fungi; GeneXpert CBNAAT for TB; CT chest (sarcoidosis, TB); serum ACE (sarcoidosis); systemic Crohn's evaluation
types.india_importance: Gastric TB must be excluded in any Indian patient with granulomatous gastritis — perform ZN stain, Mycobacterial culture, and GeneXpert before diagnosing Crohn's or sarcoid; anti-TB treatment if TB confirmed

types.name: Ménétrier's Disease (Hypertrophic Gastropathy)
types.description: A rare premalignant condition characterised by massive enlargement of gastric folds (giant rugae), foveolar hyperplasia, gland atrophy, and protein-losing gastropathy. Associated with excessive TGF-alpha (transforming growth factor alpha) signalling. Presents with: epigastric pain; severe hypoproteinaemia (protein-losing gastropathy — albumin levels very low); peripheral oedema (hypoalbuminaemia); weight loss; sometimes gastrointestinal bleeding. Increased risk of gastric cancer. In children: often caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection — self-limiting and resolves spontaneously. In adults: H. pylori may be associated; CMV in immunocompromised. Rare.
types.management: Cetuximab (anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody) — the most effective specific treatment targeting TGF-alpha/EGFR pathway; high-protein diet; albumin infusions for severe hypoalbuminaemia; H. pylori eradication; PPI; gastrectomy in refractory cases or cancer prevention

types.name: Portal Hypertensive Gastropathy (PHG)
types.description: Gastric mucosal changes caused by portal hypertension in cirrhosis — characterised by a specific endoscopic appearance (snake-skin or mosaic pattern, cherry red spots, or diffuse haemorrhagic changes) resulting from mucosal congestion, dilation of gastroduodenal mucosal capillaries, and impaired mucosal defence from portal hypertensive haemodynamic changes. PHG is not an inflammatory gastritis in the traditional sense — it is a vascular gastropathy. It is classified as mild (snake-skin/mosaic pattern alone) or severe (red marks, black-brown spots, or diffuse haemorrhagic gastric mucosa).
types.prevalence: Present in 50-80% of cirrhotic patients; more common with severe portal hypertension; increases with worsening Child-Pugh score
types.clinical_significance: Mild PHG: usually asymptomatic or causes iron-deficiency anaemia from chronic occult blood loss; Severe PHG: can cause acute or chronic GI haemorrhage (though less severe than variceal bleeding); contributes significantly to anaemia in cirrhosis
types.management: Treat underlying portal hypertension; non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol, carvedilol) — reduce portal pressure; the cornerstone of PHG management; iron supplementation for iron deficiency; transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS) for severe refractory PHG bleeding; liver transplantation for end-stage liver disease

types.name: Radiation Gastritis
types.description: Gastric mucosal injury from external beam radiation therapy to the upper abdomen (for gastric cancer, pancreatic cancer, or hepatocellular carcinoma). Radiation doses >45-50 Gy cause progressive mucosal ischaemia and fibrosis. Acute radiation gastritis (during radiation course): nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, acute mucosal erythema and erosions. Chronic radiation gastropathy (months to years later): gastric atrophy, telangiectasias (GAVE-like — dilated vessels), fibrosis, strictures, and mucosal ischaemia leading to persistent haemorrhage.
types.management: Acute: PPIs, antiemetics, dose adjustment; Chronic haemorrhage: endoscopic argon plasma coagulation (APC) for telangiectasias; sucralfate enemas; hyperbaric oxygen therapy (promotes tissue healing)

severity_levels.name: Non-Atrophic Chronic Gastritis (OLGA Stage 0-I)
severity_levels.description: Chronic active gastritis without gland loss — the most common histological finding in H. pylori-infected individuals. May be asymptomatic or cause dyspeptic symptoms.
severity_levels.criteria: Chronic active gastritis on histology; no gland atrophy; no intestinal metaplasia; H. pylori typically present; OLGA Stage 0-I
severity_levels.functional_impact: Often asymptomatic; may cause dyspepsia; no malabsorption
severity_levels.management: H. pylori eradication (curative — resolves inflammation); PPI for symptom relief if dyspeptic; lifestyle modification; no endoscopic surveillance needed after H. pylori eradication in Stage 0-I
severity_levels.prognosis: Excellent — no significant cancer risk at this stage; resolves with H. pylori eradication

severity_levels.name: Chronic Atrophic Gastritis (OLGA Stage II-III)
severity_levels.description: Chronic gastritis with loss of gastric glands in antrum or corpus — represents intermediate risk in the Correa cascade.
severity_levels.criteria: Moderate to severe gland atrophy in antrum (Stage II) or beginning in corpus (Stage III); intestinal metaplasia may be present (early); OLGA Stage II-III
severity_levels.functional_impact: Often asymptomatic; possible reduced acid secretion; possible early malabsorption of B12, iron, calcium; dyspepsia
severity_levels.management: H. pylori eradication (may partially reverse early atrophy); annual or 3-yearly endoscopic surveillance (OLGA Stage III) after H. pylori eradication; Vitamin B12 monitoring annually; iron and calcium supplementation if deficient; dietary advice (adequate antioxidants)
severity_levels.prognosis: Intermediate cancer risk — 5-8× relative risk of gastric cancer vs normal mucosa at OLGA Stage III

severity_levels.name: Advanced Atrophic Gastritis with Intestinal Metaplasia (OLGA/OLGIM Stage III-IV)
severity_levels.description: Extensive gland atrophy affecting both antrum and corpus, with intestinal metaplasia — particularly incomplete type (Type II/III intestinal metaplasia, highest cancer risk). Represents the highest premalignant risk category.
severity_levels.criteria: Severe atrophy in antrum and/or corpus; intestinal metaplasia (particularly incomplete Type II/III); OLGA/OLGIM Stage III-IV
severity_levels.functional_impact: Achlorhydria or hypochlorhydria; significant B12, iron, calcium malabsorption; multiple nutritional deficiencies; anaemia; possible early satiety
severity_levels.management: H. pylori eradication (reduces progression risk even at this stage); endoscopic surveillance every 3 years; regular B12, iron, calcium supplementation; high-dose antioxidants (Vitamin C, beta-carotene — limited evidence); proton pump inhibitor usually not needed (achlorhydric); close follow-up for dysplasia
severity_levels.prognosis: High cancer risk (OLGIM Stage III-IV: 50-60× relative risk of gastric cancer); 5-year cancer incidence approximately 5-10%

severity_levels.name: Gastric Dysplasia (Low-Grade and High-Grade)
severity_levels.description: Precancerous lesion characterised by histological atypia — nuclear enlargement, hyperchromatism, increased mitoses, architectural gland abnormalities — without invasion through the basement membrane. The immediate precursor to invasive gastric adenocarcinoma.
severity_levels.criteria: LOW-GRADE DYSPLASIA (LGD): mild architectural and cytological atypia; HIGH-GRADE DYSPLASIA (HGD): severe atypia approaching carcinoma; confirmed by histopathology (at least two pathologists should assess HGD)
severity_levels.cancer_risk: LGD: 0-23% progress to HGD or cancer within 5 years; HGD: 60-90% progress to invasive cancer if not treated
severity_levels.management: LOW-GRADE DYSPLASIA: endoscopic resection if visible lesion (endoscopic mucosal resection — EMR or endoscopic submucosal dissection — ESD); endoscopic surveillance every 12 months; H. pylori eradication; HIGH-GRADE DYSPLASIA: MANDATORY endoscopic or surgical resection (EMR/ESD if limited; gastrectomy for extensive); HGD is treated as early cancer in many guidelines

causative_agents_overview.h_pylori: Most important and prevalent — responsible for ~90% of all chronic gastritis; 70-80% prevalence in India; initiates the Correa cascade to gastric cancer
causative_agents_overview.nsaids_aspirin: Second most important; chemical/reactive gastropathy; direct mucosal toxicity; impair prostaglandin-mediated mucosal defence
causative_agents_overview.autoimmune: T-cell and antibody-mediated destruction of parietal cells; causes corpus atrophy; pernicious anaemia
causative_agents_overview.alcohol: Direct cytotoxicity; increases mucosal permeability; causes acute erosive and chronic reactive gastritis
causative_agents_overview.stress: Mucosal ischaemia in critically ill patients; acutely dangerous in ICU
causative_agents_overview.bile_reflux: Bile acids directly cytotoxic; chemical gastropathy; after gastric surgery or with poor pyloric function
causative_agents_overview.other: Radiation; eosinophilic (allergic); granulomatous (Crohn's, TB, sarcoid); CMV (immunocompromised)

risk_factors: H. pylori infection — the dominant and most important risk factor for all chronic gastritis in India; acquired in childhood through contaminated water, food, and person-to-person contact
Age — risk of atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia increases progressively with age; autoimmune gastritis peaks after age 50
Female sex — autoimmune gastritis 3× more common in women
Family history of gastric cancer or atrophic gastritis — genetic predisposition to H. pylori virulence response; autoimmune gastritis familial clustering
CagA-positive H. pylori strain — strongly associated with more aggressive gastritis, higher atrophy risk, higher gastric cancer risk; CagA-positive strains predominate in India
High dietary salt intake — high salt damages gastric mucosa and promotes H. pylori virulence (upregulates CagA expression); strongly associated with gastric cancer risk
Smoking — worsens H. pylori gastritis; impairs mucosal healing; increases gastric cancer risk; reduces eradication success rates
Alcohol — direct mucosal irritant; inhibits prostaglandin synthesis; worsens NSAIDs gastropathy synergistically
NSAID and aspirin use — direct and indirect mucosal injury; increases gastritis severity in H. pylori-infected individuals
Stress — acute physiological stress (ICU admission, major surgery, severe burns) triggers stress gastritis; psychological stress exacerbates functional gastric symptoms
Genetic polymorphisms — IL-1B (-511) and IL-1RA VNTR gene polymorphisms increase hypochlorhydria and gastric cancer risk in H. pylori-infected individuals
Bile reflux — post-gastrectomy; post-pyloroplasty; occasionally without prior surgery

Autoimmune diseases — patients with type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, Addison's disease, or Sjögren's syndrome have significantly higher risk of autoimmune gastritis (autoimmune polyglandular syndrome)
Low socioeconomic status — correlates with H. pylori acquisition risk in India through poor WASH access
Low dietary antioxidant intake — low Vitamin C, beta-carotene, selenium intake increases progression risk from gastritis to cancer
Blood group A — 20-25% higher gastric cancer risk (associated with specific mucosal carbohydrate expression favouring cancer progression)

symptoms.overview: One of the most clinically important concepts in gastritis is the profound DISSOCIATION between histological disease severity and symptoms. The majority of patients with histologically confirmed chronic gastritis — even severe atrophic gastritis — are COMPLETELY ASYMPTOMATIC. Conversely, many patients with severe dyspeptic symptoms have an entirely normal gastric mucosa (functional dyspepsia). This means gastritis is usually a histopathological and endoscopic diagnosis, not a clinical diagnosis based on symptoms alone. The symptoms listed below are those that MAY occur in gastritis but are non-specific and overlap extensively with peptic ulcer disease, GERD, functional dyspepsia, and biliary disease.

primary_symptoms.name: Epigastric Pain and Discomfort
primary_symptoms.description: Dull, burning, aching, or pressure-like pain or discomfort in the upper middle abdomen (epigastrium) — the most common symptom when present. In H. pylori gastritis: pain may be worsened or relieved by eating (variable — no consistent pattern distinguishing it from peptic ulcer); worse on lying flat; may radiate to the back. In autoimmune gastritis: epigastric pain is often mild or absent despite severe mucosal atrophy. In acute erosive gastritis (NSAIDs, alcohol): pain onset is more acute, sometimes severe. Character: burning, gnawing, or 'empty stomach' sensation.
primary_symptoms.onset: Acute gastritis: sudden; Chronic gastritis: gradual, waxing and waning over months to years
primary_symptoms.note: The location (epigastric), character (burning), and temporal patterns of gastritis pain are indistinguishable from peptic ulcer disease, GERD, and functional dyspepsia — endoscopy with biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis

primary_symptoms.name: Nausea and Vomiting
primary_symptoms.description: Nausea — often the dominant symptom in acute gastritis; may be persistent or intermittent; worse in the morning or after eating. Vomiting occurs in more severe acute gastritis (alcohol, NSAIDs) and in acute H. pylori gastritis at onset of infection. In chronic gastritis: vomiting is less common — significant vomiting with chronic gastritis should raise concern for gastroparesis, pyloric stenosis, or gastric cancer. In autoimmune gastritis with severe achlorhydria: early satiety and nausea may result from impaired gastric emptying (achlorhydria reduces the acid stimulus for gastric motility).
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Moderate in chronic; Moderate to Severe in acute

primary_symptoms.name: Anorexia and Early Satiety
primary_symptoms.description: Loss of appetite (anorexia) is common in acute gastritis (cytokinemia, nausea). In chronic atrophic gastritis: reduced acid production → impaired gastric emptying → early satiety; protein malabsorption and zinc deficiency (both occur in achlorhydria) further impair appetite. Early satiety or marked and persistent anorexia with weight loss in a patient with chronic gastritis is an ALARM FEATURE — must rule out gastric cancer.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild in most; Severe early satiety with weight loss = alarm feature
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Weight loss + early satiety + epigastric pain + gastritis in a patient over 50 = urgent endoscopy to exclude gastric cancer

primary_symptoms.name: Haematemesis and Melaena (Acute Erosive Gastritis)
primary_symptoms.description: Vomiting of blood (haematemesis — fresh red or coffee-ground appearance) or passing black tarry stools (melaena — digested blood) indicates upper GI bleeding from acute erosive gastritis. Most commonly from: NSAID or aspirin use; alcohol; stress gastritis in ICU. Erosive gastritis bleeding is usually low-volume and self-limiting but can occasionally be life-threatening, particularly in critically ill patients or those on anticoagulants. Any haematemesis or melaena requires urgent endoscopy.
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: HAEMATEMESIS IS AN EMERGENCY — urgent endoscopy within 24 hours (emergency endoscopy if haemodynamically compromised)

primary_symptoms.name: Symptoms of B12 and Iron Deficiency (Autoimmune Gastritis)
primary_symptoms.description: Autoimmune gastritis is OFTEN SILENT for decades — presenting only through the complications of nutrient malabsorption: VITAMIN B12 DEFICIENCY: megaloblastic anaemia (fatigue, pallor, macrocytic anaemia); neurological manifestations — subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord (symmetrical limb weakness, spasticity, ataxia, loss of proprioception — progressive and irreversible if untreated); peripheral neuropathy (tingling, numbness in hands and feet); psychiatric symptoms (depression, cognitive impairment, dementia); glossitis (sore, smooth red tongue — loss of papillae). IRON DEFICIENCY: microcytic hypochromic anaemia; fatigue; brittle nails; hair loss; spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia); pica (unusual food cravings). CALCIUM DEFICIENCY: osteoporosis; tetany.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild (early — anaemia) to Severe (neurological — irreversible if untreated)
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Any patient with UNEXPLAINED B12 DEFICIENCY, PERNICIOUS ANAEMIA, or UNEXPLAINED IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA should be investigated for autoimmune gastritis (anti-parietal cell antibodies, serum gastrin, gastroscopy with biopsy)

secondary_symptoms: Bloating and fullness after eating — impaired gastric emptying from achlorhydria; gas accumulation
Belching (eructation) — aerophagia from nausea; impaired gastric motility; gas production
Heartburn and acid regurgitation — may coexist with gastritis from GERD overlap
Halitosis (bad breath) — H. pylori produces volatile sulphur compounds; also from undigested food in achlorhydric stomach
Weight loss — reduced food intake from nausea and anorexia; malabsorption in severe atrophic gastritis; ALARM FEATURE if significant
Fatigue and pallor — from anaemia (B12, iron, or blood loss in erosive gastritis)
Tingling or numbness in hands and feet — early B12 deficiency peripheral neuropathy in autoimmune gastritis
Glossitis — smooth, red, 'beefy' tongue from B12 deficiency
Jaundice (mild) — haemolytic component of pernicious anaemia (RBC destruction from ineffective erythropoiesis)
alarm_features_requiring_urgent_endoscop: Haematemesis or melaena (vomiting blood or black tarry stools) — urgent endoscopy within 24 hours
Unexplained significant weight loss (>3 kg or >5% body weight) with gastric symptoms
Persistent vomiting (possible gastric outlet obstruction from ulcer or cancer)
Iron deficiency anaemia without other explanation in patients over 50 years
Age ≥55 years with new onset or recent change in gastric symptoms
Family history of gastric cancer in first-degree relative with gastric symptoms
Symptoms not responding to 8 weeks of appropriate treatment
Any combination of alarm features: weight loss + anaemia + epigastric pain = gastric cancer until proven otherwise

medical_history: Symptom characterisation — epigastric pain or discomfort; burning vs cramping vs pressure-like; relationship to meals (before, during, or after eating); relieving and aggravating factors; duration and frequency; nocturnal symptoms (peptic ulcer typically wakes patient at night)
Duration of symptoms — acute (days: alcohol, NSAID) vs chronic (months-years: H. pylori, autoimmune)

NSAID and aspirin use — current and past; type and dose; frequency; OTC analgesic use (ibuprofen, diclofenac, aspirin — very commonly underreported in India); duration of use; any PPI gastroprotection co-prescribed
Alcohol consumption — amount, frequency, duration; recent heavy binge drinking (acute haemorrhagic gastritis)
H. pylori testing and treatment history — ever tested? By what method? If positive, was treatment given? What regimen? Was test-of-cure performed?
Family history — first-degree relatives with gastric cancer; peptic ulcer disease; pernicious anaemia; autoimmune diseases

Personal autoimmune history — Type 1 diabetes; autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves'); Addison's disease; vitiligo; Sjögren's syndrome (triggers autoimmune gastritis investigation)
Neurological symptoms — tingling, numbness, weakness in limbs; balance difficulties; memory changes (B12 deficiency from autoimmune gastritis)
Anaemia symptoms — breathlessness, palpitations, fatigue; pallor; recent haematological workup
Weight loss — amount and duration; intentional or unintentional
Prior gastric surgery — partial gastrectomy (Billroth I or II) predisposes to bile reflux gastropathy; pyloroplasty; vagotomy
Previous endoscopy — when; what was found; biopsies taken; H. pylori status

Medication history — full medication list including herbal preparations; iron supplements (can cause chemical gastropathy); potassium chloride; metformin; immunosuppressants (CMV gastritis risk); chemotherapy/radiation history
TB history or contact — granulomatous gastritis in India; Mycobacterium TB must be excluded
ICU admission — critically ill patients → stress gastritis; recent major surgery, severe burns, or trauma
Geographic and dietary history — high-salt diet (increases gastric cancer risk); low fruit and vegetable intake; Gangetic belt residence (very high gastric cancer + gallbladder cancer region)
physical_examination: Vital signs — heart rate (tachycardia in bleeding or severe illness); blood pressure (hypotension = significant haemorrhage); temperature (fever in acute gastritis or complicated infection)

General appearance — pallor (anaemia — B12 deficiency in autoimmune; iron deficiency from erosive gastritis or H. pylori-related malabsorption); jaundice (pernicious anaemia — mild haemolysis); nutritional status; body weight

Tongue examination — GLOSSITIS (smooth, beefy, red tongue — loss of papillae from B12 deficiency; very specific for megaloblastic anaemia from pernicious anaemia or nutritional B12 deficiency); geographic tongue (non-specific); angular cheilitis (B12 or iron deficiency)
Nail changes — koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails — iron deficiency); pallor of nail bed (anaemia)

Neurological examination — particularly important in suspected autoimmune gastritis: proprioception (Romberg's test — loss of joint position sense = subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord); vibration sense (tuning fork at ankles); coordination; deep tendon reflexes (brisk in early SCD; may be decreased in peripheral neuropathy); cognitive assessment
INSPECTION: epigastric fullness or distension; visible peristalsis (gastric outlet obstruction)

PALPATION: epigastric tenderness (mild to moderate in gastritis); epigastric mass (ALARM SIGN — gastric cancer; pancreatic mass); hepatomegaly; splenomegaly (portal hypertension in PHG; lymphoma in MALT lymphoma)

AUSCULTATION: succussion splash (gastric outlet obstruction — delayed gastric emptying; patient is rocked side to side while clinician auscultates over epigastrium — splashing sound indicates retained gastric contents hours after last meal)

Lymphadenopathy — supraclavicular (Virchow's/Troisier's node = gastric cancer or lymphoma metastasis); axillary (Sister Mary Joseph's nodule is umbilical metastatic deposit — late gastric cancer sign)
Skin — vitiligo (associated with autoimmune gastritis); features of Addison's disease (hyperpigmentation); thyroid enlargement (autoimmune thyroid disease associated with autoimmune gastritis)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Upper GI Endoscopy (OGD/EGD) with Biopsy — Gold Standard
diagnostic_tests.description: The definitive investigation for diagnosing gastritis — providing both macroscopic (endoscopic) and microscopic (histopathological) assessment. Macroscopic endoscopic findings in gastritis include: erythema (redness); mucosal oedema; erosions (small mucosal breaks <5 mm without depth — distinguishing from ulcers); haemorrhagic spots or stigmata; nodularity (cobblestone appearance in H. pylori gastritis); flat or raised mucosal lesions; visible blood vessels (atrophy); intestinal metaplasia (pale, irregular, flat mucosa with grey-white patches or irregular geography); Endoscopic view of gastric folds: enlarged giant rugal folds (Ménétrier's); flattened thin folds (atrophy). BIOPSY IS MANDATORY — endoscopic appearance correlates poorly with histological severity; systematic biopsy from 5 sites using the Sydney protocol (antrum greater curvature, antrum lesser curvature, incisura angularis, corpus greater curvature, corpus lesser curvature — minimum 5 biopsies) allows accurate histological grading by the Sydney and OLGA systems.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose gastritis type (H. pylori, autoimmune, chemical, eosinophilic); stage atrophy and intestinal metaplasia (OLGA/OLGIM); detect dysplasia and cancer; CLO test for H. pylori; assess complications
diagnostic_tests.what_biopsies_show: H. pylori gastritis: H. pylori organisms visible on H&E or Giemsa stain; neutrophilic and mononuclear infiltrate; Autoimmune gastritis: corpus-predominant gland atrophy; mononuclear infiltrate; ECL hyperplasia; intestinal metaplasia; Chemical gastropathy: foveolar hyperplasia; minimal inflammation; smooth muscle fibres in lamina propria; Eosinophilic gastritis: ≥30 eosinophils/HPF; Granulomatous: epithelioid granulomas with or without caseation (TB vs non-TB)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: OLGA/OLGIM staging from histology guides cancer surveillance intervals; H. pylori status (CLO test + histology); presence and grade of intestinal metaplasia (complete vs incomplete)
diagnostic_tests.preparation: Stop PPIs for 2 weeks before endoscopy if H. pylori CLO test is planned; stop bismuth and antibiotics for 4 weeks; endoscopy under conscious sedation; fasting from midnight
diagnostic_tests.india_note: OGD with biopsy available at all urban hospitals in India; cost Rs 2,000-8,000 at government vs private hospitals; essential investigation for any alarm feature gastric symptom; OLGA staging increasingly performed at tertiary centres

diagnostic_tests.test_name: H. pylori Urea Breath Test (UBT) — Gold Standard Non-Invasive
diagnostic_tests.description: The most accurate non-invasive test for active H. pylori infection — 13C-labelled urea is ingested; H. pylori urease cleaves it to 13CO2 detectable in breath. Sensitivity and specificity >95%. Most appropriate for diagnosing H. pylori in the community setting before endoscopy, and for confirming eradication after treatment (test of cure — minimum 4 weeks after completing antibiotics, 2 weeks off PPIs).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose active H. pylori infection; confirm eradication (test of cure) — most important post-treatment test
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive = active H. pylori infection; sensitivity >95%; specificity >95%
diagnostic_tests.preparation_critical: Stop PPIs for minimum 2 weeks before test; stop H2 blockers for 48 hours; stop antibiotics and bismuth for 4 weeks; take test fasting or after light non-dairy breakfast

diagnostic_tests.description: Monoclonal antibody-based test detecting H. pylori antigens in stool. Accuracy comparable to UBT (sensitivity ~94%, specificity ~97%). Useful when UBT equipment unavailable; very useful for children; equally valid for test of cure.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose active H. pylori; test of cure post-treatment; suitable for children and elderly; less equipment-dependent than UBT

diagnostic_tests.test_name: CLO Test (Campylobacter-Like Organism / Rapid Urease Test) at Endoscopy
diagnostic_tests.description: Rapid urease test on gastric antral biopsy taken at endoscopy — H. pylori urease converts urea to ammonia raising pH and changing colour indicator. Results in 1-3 hours. Sensitivity 85-98%, specificity 95-100%.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Rapid diagnosis of H. pylori at time of endoscopy; complemented by histological staining of same biopsy material
diagnostic_tests.note: False negative if: on PPIs (H. pylori suppressed); on recent antibiotics; heavy bleeding in stomach (haematocrit lowers sensitivity); always send biopsies for histology as well

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Anti-Parietal Cell Antibodies (APCA) and Anti-Intrinsic Factor Antibodies (AIFA)
diagnostic_tests.description: Serological markers for autoimmune gastritis. Anti-parietal cell antibodies (APCA): directed against the H+/K+-ATPase proton pump; sensitivity 90% for autoimmune gastritis; specificity LOW (present in 10-15% of healthy adults — particularly elderly women; also in Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease without gastric disease); positive APCA alone is not diagnostic. Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (AIFA): Type 1 blocking antibody (prevents B12 binding to IF) and Type 2 binding antibody (prevents IF-B12 complex ileal absorption); sensitivity only 50-70% but SPECIFICITY >95% — highly specific when positive; detecting AIFA in a patient with B12 deficiency is virtually diagnostic of autoimmune gastritis/pernicious anaemia.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for and diagnose autoimmune gastritis; investigate unexplained B12 deficiency, pernicious anaemia, or unexplained iron deficiency anaemia
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: APCA positive + AIFA positive (either type) = DIAGNOSTIC of autoimmune gastritis/pernicious anaemia with >95% certainty; APCA positive + AIFA negative = possible autoimmune gastritis — confirm with endoscopy and gastrin; AIFA positive = highly specific for pernicious anaemia regardless of APCA

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Gastrin and Pepsinogen I / Pepsinogen I:II Ratio
diagnostic_tests.description: Non-invasive serology markers for gastric mucosal atrophy: SERUM GASTRIN: produced by G cells in the antrum; released in response to alkaline stomach pH (loss of acid negative feedback); MARKEDLY ELEVATED (>200 pg/mL; often >500-2000 pg/mL) in autoimmune gastritis (achlorhydria removes acid-mediated feedback inhibition of G cells; the antrum is spared in autoimmune gastritis so G cells are preserved and hyperactive); moderately elevated in H. pylori corpus gastritis (with concurrent hypochlorhydria). PEPSINOGEN I (PGI): produced exclusively by chief cells in the gastric body/corpus; falls with corpus atrophy — very low PGI (<70 mcg/L) suggests corpus atrophy; PEPSINOGEN I/II RATIO: PGI/PGII ratio <3 (particularly <2) strongly suggests advanced corpus atrophy (sensitivity 70-80%; specificity 90% for detecting OLGIM Stage III-IV). Marketed as the 'serological biopsy' for gastric cancer screening in Japan and parts of Asia.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose autoimmune gastritis (elevated gastrin); screen for corpus atrophy (low PGI, low PGI/PGII ratio); non-invasive triage before endoscopy; serial monitoring of atrophy progression
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Serum gastrin >200 pg/mL: possible autoimmune gastritis or ZES (Zollinger-Ellison); >500 pg/mL: highly suggestive of autoimmune gastritis or ZES; PGI <70 mcg/L + PGI/PGII ratio <3 = significant corpus atrophy present
diagnostic_tests.india_note: Serum gastrin and pepsinogen testing increasingly available at major Indian diagnostic centres; important for non-invasive initial assessment of gastric atrophy risk

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Vitamin B12 and Methylmalonic Acid (MMA)
diagnostic_tests.description: Assessment of B12 status — critical in autoimmune gastritis screening and monitoring. Serum B12: <200 pg/mL = deficient; 200-300 pg/mL = borderline (check functional markers). Methylmalonic acid (MMA): elevated in B12 deficiency even before serum B12 falls below normal range — a more sensitive marker of FUNCTIONAL B12 deficiency; MMA accumulates when B12 is inadequate for the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase enzyme. Homocysteine: also elevated in B12 deficiency (and folate deficiency) — less specific. In autoimmune gastritis: B12 falls very slowly over years (large hepatic stores); MMA elevation may precede overt anaemia by years.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for B12 deficiency in autoimmune gastritis; monitor B12 replacement therapy; detect early functional deficiency before overt pernicious anaemia develops
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: B12 <200 pg/mL = deficient; MMA >0.4 mcmol/L = functional B12 deficiency (most sensitive marker); Homocysteine >15 mcmol/L = B12 or folate deficiency

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Full Blood Count (FBC) and Blood Film
diagnostic_tests.description: Essential for detecting anaemia in gastritis: MACROCYTIC ANAEMIA (high MCV >100 fL): B12 or folate deficiency (autoimmune gastritis — pernicious anaemia); hypersegmented neutrophils on blood film (CHARACTERISTIC of megaloblastic anaemia — neutrophils have ≥5 lobes); oval macrocytes; MICROCYTIC ANAEMIA (low MCV, low ferritin): iron deficiency from H. pylori-related iron malabsorption, chronic mucosal blood loss (erosive gastritis), or achlorhydria (acid required for iron absorption); MIXED DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA: combined B12 + iron deficiency → can result in 'normal' MCV masking megaloblastic anaemia — blood film showing dimorphic population (mixed macrocytes and microcytes) is the clue.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect and characterise anaemia type; screen for pernicious anaemia; detect iron deficiency; identify mixed deficiency (B12 + iron)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: MCV >100 + hypersegmented neutrophils = megaloblastic anaemia → investigate B12/folate; MCV <80 + low ferritin = iron deficiency → investigate cause

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Iron Studies (Serum Ferritin, Transferrin, Serum Iron, TIBC)
diagnostic_tests.description: H. pylori gastritis is an important and underrecognised cause of iron deficiency anaemia — even without visible GI blood loss. Mechanisms: H. pylori competes with the host for iron (H. pylori has iron-acquisition virulence factors — lactoferrin binding protein); H. pylori gastritis reduces ascorbic acid levels in gastric juice (Vitamin C normally converts ferric to ferrous iron for absorption); H. pylori-induced achlorhydria (particularly corpus atrophy) impairs acid-dependent ferric-to-ferrous conversion required for iron absorption. H. pylori eradication may resolve iron deficiency anaemia without iron supplementation in some patients.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm iron deficiency; assess severity and response to supplementation; monitor after H. pylori eradication (may improve without iron supplementation if H. pylori eradication restores normal iron absorption)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Ferritin <15 mcg/L = iron deficient; ferritin 15-30 = functional iron deficiency; TIBC elevated; transferrin saturation <20%

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Chromogranin A and Gastric Neuroendocrine Tumour Screening
diagnostic_tests.description: Chromogranin A (CgA) is a secretory protein produced by neuroendocrine cells — elevated in neuroendocrine tumours (NETs). Relevant in autoimmune gastritis (Type 1 gastric NETs from ECL cell hyperplasia) and in Ménétrier's disease surveillance. In autoimmune gastritis: serum CgA elevated (reflecting ECL cell hyperplasia and carcinoid tumour activity). NOTE: PPIs are a major confounding cause of CgA elevation (PPIs cause hypergastrinaemia → ECL stimulation → CgA elevation — always stop PPIs for 2 weeks before CgA testing).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for gastric neuroendocrine tumours in autoimmune gastritis; monitoring after resection of Type 1 gastric NETs
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CgA >upper limit of normal (lab-specific) after PPI washout = possible NET activity

diagnostic_tests.description: Imaging is NOT routinely required for uncomplicated gastritis — this is a mucosal disease diagnosed by endoscopy and histology. However, imaging is indicated for: suspected gastric cancer (CT staging — tumour extent, lymph nodes, distant metastases, liver); granulomatous gastritis (CT chest for sarcoidosis, pulmonary TB); suspected pancreatitis or biliary disease as a differential diagnosis; MALT lymphoma staging (CT abdomen with contrast); severe Ménétrier's disease with suspected malignancy; portal hypertensive gastropathy (hepatic and portal venous assessment).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Cancer staging (gastric cancer); differential diagnosis; lymphoma staging
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CT: gastric wall thickening >1 cm; regional lymphadenopathy; hepatic metastases — all suggest gastric cancer; linitis plastica (diffuse infiltrative gastric cancer — 'leather bottle' stomach)

medicines.note: Treatment of gastritis is fundamentally aetiological — the most effective management targets the underlying cause rather than providing only symptomatic acid suppression. H. pylori eradication is the most important pharmacological intervention for H. pylori gastritis — it resolves mucosal inflammation, heals peptic ulcers, reduces gastric cancer risk, and may reverse early atrophy. Vitamin B12 replacement is the specific treatment for autoimmune gastritis. Acid suppression (PPIs) is appropriate for symptomatic relief, NSAID gastroprotection, peptic ulcer healing, and as a component of H. pylori eradication — but long-term empirical PPI use without a defined indication should be avoided.
treatment_principles: 1. TREAT THE CAUSE: H. pylori → ERADICATE; NSAID-induced → STOP or CO-PRESCRIBE PPI; autoimmune → B12 replacement + surveillance; alcohol → CESSATION; stress → PROPHYLAXIS in ICU high-risk patients
2. H. PYLORI ERADICATION is the cornerstone of H. pylori gastritis management — not symptom suppression with PPIs alone; confirm eradication with UBT or stool antigen at 4+ weeks post-treatment

3. ACID SUPPRESSION (PPIs) is appropriate for: NSAID gastroprotection; acute symptomatic relief; peptic ulcer healing; H. pylori eradication (as part of the regimen); stress ulcer prophylaxis in high-risk ICU; NOT for long-term indefinite use in asymptomatic gastritis

4. MUCOSAL PROTECTIVE AGENTS (sucralfate, bismuth, rebamipide) address the defensive side of the acid-mucosal barrier equation — valuable adjuncts particularly in chemical gastropathy and as H. pylori eradication components
5. REGULAR REVIEW AND DEPRESCRIBING of PPIs — reassess at every consultation; the majority of patients on long-term PPIs in India have no documented indication; step down or stop when appropriate
6. AUTOIMMUNE GASTRITIS: B12 replacement via IM injection is mandatory; monitor annually for gastric cancer and type 1 NETs; do not use PPIs (achlorhydric — no acid to suppress)

categories.category_name: H. pylori Eradication Therapy — See also DIS-021 Dyspepsia
categories.purpose: Eradicate H. pylori infection — resolves chronic gastritis, reduces peptic ulcer risk, reduces gastric cancer risk, and may improve dyspeptic symptoms in H. pylori-positive patients.
categories.treatment_duration: 14 days preferred (10 days minimum); 7-day regimens are no longer recommended due to inadequate eradication rates
categories.test_of_cure: MANDATORY — UBT or stool antigen minimum 4 weeks after completing antibiotics (2 weeks off PPIs) to confirm eradication
categories.india_resistance_context: Clarithromycin resistance in India rising (15-30% in many centres); metronidazole resistance very high (50-80%); fluoroquinolone resistance rising; bismuth quadruple therapy increasingly preferred in India as first-line given high clarithromycin and metronidazole resistance rates

regimens.name: Bismuth-Based Quadruple Therapy (BQT) — PREFERRED FIRST-LINE IN INDIA
regimens.components: PPI (standard dose twice daily) + Bismuth subcitrate 120-240 mg four times daily + Metronidazole 400 mg three to four times daily + Tetracycline 500 mg four times daily × 14 days
regimens.eradication_rate: 85-95%; remains high even in areas of metronidazole resistance (bismuth has direct bactericidal activity independent of antibiotic mechanisms)
regimens.india_rationale: Preferred in India due to: high clarithromycin resistance rendering standard triple therapy less effective; bismuth direct anti-H. pylori activity overcoming metronidazole resistance to some extent; widely available at low cost; recommended by Indian Society of Gastroenterology
regimens.note: Bismuth salts cause black stools and black tongue — harmless bismuth sulphide; warn patients; tetracycline avoid in pregnancy and children <12 years

regimens.name: Standard Triple Therapy (PPI + Clarithromycin + Amoxicillin)
regimens.components: PPI (standard dose twice daily) + Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily + Amoxicillin 1g twice daily × 14 days
regimens.eradication_rate: 70-85% in low-clarithromycin-resistance areas; significantly lower in India where clarithromycin resistance is 15-30%
regimens.note: If penicillin allergy: replace amoxicillin with metronidazole 400 mg twice daily; increasingly less reliable in India

regimens.name: Second-Line (Salvage) After Failed First-Line
options: Levofloxacin-based triple: PPI + Levofloxacin 500 mg once daily + Amoxicillin 1g twice daily × 10-14 days
Bismuth quadruple therapy (if not used as first-line)
After two failures: culture and sensitivity testing of H. pylori strongly recommended; rifabutin-based therapy for multiply-treated patients (avoid in TB-endemic settings without ruling out TB)

medicines_in_eradication_regimens.name: Omeprazole / Pantoprazole / Esomeprazole / Rabeprazole
medicines_in_eradication_regimens.dosage: Standard dose twice daily during H. pylori eradication (omeprazole 20 mg twice daily; pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily; esomeprazole 40 mg twice daily; rabeprazole 20 mg twice daily)
medicines_in_eradication_regimens.note: Rabeprazole may be slightly superior for H. pylori eradication due to less CYP2C19-dependent metabolism — more consistent acid suppression across genetic metaboliser types

medicines_in_eradication_regimens.name: Bismuth Subcitrate (De-Nol)
medicines_in_eradication_regimens.dosage: 120 mg four times daily (half-hour before meals and at bedtime) OR 240 mg twice daily
medicines_in_eradication_regimens.mechanism: Direct bactericidal activity against H. pylori (disrupts bacterial cell wall and metabolism independent of urease inhibition); forms a protective coating over inflamed gastric mucosa (cytoprotective); anti-adhesive (prevents H. pylori from binding to gastric epithelium); synergistic with antibiotics — overcomes antibiotic resistance to some degree
medicines_in_eradication_regimens.additional_benefits: Mucosal protective (coating effect); anti-pepsin activity; stimulates prostaglandin and mucus synthesis; used as monotherapy for mild dyspepsia in some guidelines

categories.purpose: Suppress gastric acid secretion to: (1) relieve dyspeptic symptoms from gastritis; (2) heal peptic ulcers; (3) provide gastroprotection during NSAID therapy; (4) as part of H. pylori eradication regimens; (5) stress ulcer prophylaxis in high-risk ICU patients.

medicines.name: Omeprazole
medicines.form: Capsule (10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg); IV injection
medicines.dosage: Gastritis symptom relief: 20 mg once daily before breakfast × 4-8 weeks; Peptic ulcer: 20-40 mg once daily × 4-8 weeks; NSAID gastroprotection: 20 mg once daily; H. pylori eradication component: 20 mg twice daily × 14 days; ICU stress ulcer prophylaxis: 40 mg IV once or twice daily
medicines.mechanism: Irreversible inhibition of H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) after acid activation in gastric parietal cell canaliculi; inhibits acid secretion by 90-98%; take 30-60 minutes before first meal for maximum efficacy
medicines.long_term_risks: B12 deficiency (impairs food-protein-bound B12 absorption — crystalline cyanocobalamin supplements still absorbed); magnesium deficiency (hypomagnesaemia — risk of arrhythmia); C. difficile infection (increased 2×); community-acquired pneumonia; fracture risk (reduced calcium absorption); renal disease (interstitial nephritis); rebound acid hypersecretion on discontinuation
medicines.deprescribing: Taper when stopping long-term PPIs: reduce to 20 mg on alternate days for 2-4 weeks → stop; this prevents rebound acid hypersecretion (which can cause transient dyspepsia and heartburn — paradoxically making patients think they still need the PPI)

medicines.name: Pantoprazole
medicines.dosage: Gastritis: 40 mg once daily; IV for acute bleeding: 80 mg bolus + 8 mg/hour infusion × 72 hours post-endoscopic haemostasis
medicines.note: Fewer drug interactions than omeprazole (less CYP2C19 inhibition); preferred when patient is on clopidogrel (reduced CYP2C19 interaction)

medicines.name: Rabeprazole
medicines.advantage: Less affected by CYP2C19 genetic polymorphism — most consistent acid suppression regardless of metaboliser status; may be superior for H. pylori eradication

medicines.name: Esomeprazole
medicines.note: S-isomer of omeprazole; marginally superior for erosive oesophagitis healing; higher cost than generic omeprazole

categories.purpose: Moderate acid suppression — less potent than PPIs; used for mild gastritis, break-through symptoms, or as alternative to PPIs when PPIs are not tolerated or are being deprescribed.

medicines.name: Famotidine
medicines.dosage: 20 mg twice daily or 40 mg once daily at night; PRN: 10-20 mg as needed for breakthrough symptoms
medicines.use_case: Mild gastritis symptoms; PRN use for breakthrough heartburn; alternative to PPI in mild GERD; H2 blocker prophylaxis in lower-risk ICU patients; useful during PPI deprescription process as a step-down
medicines.advantages_over_ppi: Faster onset of action (30-60 minutes vs 1-2 hours for PPI); no significant drug interactions; no rebound acid hypersecretion on discontinuation; OTC availability; appropriate for PRN use
medicines.limitation: Tachyphylaxis (tolerance) develops within 2-3 weeks of continuous use — efficacy diminishes with regular around-the-clock use

categories.purpose: Enhance gastric mucosal defence mechanisms rather than reducing acid output — complementary to or alternative to acid suppression in gastritis management.

medicines.name: Sucralfate
medicines.dosage: 1 g four times daily on an empty stomach (1 hour before meals and at bedtime) OR 2 g twice daily; take with water; separate from other medications by 2 hours
medicines.use_case: Gastritis and peptic ulcer healing; NSAID-induced gastropathy; stress ulcer prophylaxis in ICU (alternative to PPI — particularly appropriate when C. difficile or pneumonia risk from PPI is a concern); oesophagitis; bile reflux gastropathy; safe in pregnancy
medicines.mechanism: Polyanionic aluminium sucrose sulphate — in acidic environment forms a viscous adhesive paste that binds to positively charged proteins in ulcer/erosion base; forms a physical barrier protecting eroded mucosa from acid, pepsin, and bile; stimulates prostaglandin E2 synthesis (cytoprotective); promotes bicarbonate and mucus secretion; binds epidermal growth factor (EGF) concentrating it at mucosal injury site
medicines.note: Requires acid for activation — less effective with concurrent PPI use (PPI raises pH, impairing sucralfate activation); must be taken on empty stomach; can reduce absorption of fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, digoxin, warfarin, phenytoin, and thyroid hormones — separate by 2 hours

medicines.name: Rebamipide
medicines.dosage: 100 mg three times daily (or twice daily)
medicines.use_case: Widely used in Japan, South Korea, and increasingly India for gastric mucosal protection in gastritis; H. pylori gastritis (augments mucosal defence while awaiting eradication); NSAID-induced gastropathy (enhances mucosal prostaglandin synthesis and mucus production); improves gastric mucosal healing post-H. pylori eradication
medicines.mechanism: Increases gastric mucosal prostaglandin E2 and I2 synthesis (cytoprotective prostaglandins); stimulates mucous secretion; scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS — protective against oxidative stress-mediated mucosal injury); enhances tight junction protein expression; anti-inflammatory (reduces IL-8 and TNF-alpha in gastric mucosa)
medicines.evidence: Multiple Japanese RCTs show rebamipide accelerates gastric mucosal healing post-H. pylori eradication; reduces NSAID-induced small bowel injury; reduces upper GI adverse events from NSAIDs
medicines.india_availability: Increasingly available at urban pharmacies in India; generic versions from Indian manufacturers

medicines.name: Misoprostol (Prostaglandin E1 Analogue) — NSAID Gastroprotection
medicines.dosage: 200 mcg four times daily with food
medicines.use_case: Prevention of NSAID-induced gastric and duodenal ulcers and erosions; replaces prostaglandins depleted by COX-1 inhibition from NSAIDs; evidence-based NSAID gastroprotection; reduces NSAID-related GI complications by 40-50%
medicines.mechanism: Exogenous PGE1 replaces depleted mucosal prostaglandins; stimulates mucus and bicarbonate secretion; enhances mucosal blood flow; reduces acid secretion (partial H+/K+-ATPase inhibition)
medicines.side_effects: Diarrhoea and abdominal cramps (most common — 20-30%; dose-related); nausea; UTEROTONIC: ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION in pregnancy (causes miscarriage and premature labour)
medicines.note: Poor tolerability limits use — PPIs are better tolerated for NSAID gastroprotection

medicines.name: Bismuth Subcitrate (as Mucosal Protectant)
medicines.dosage: 120 mg four times daily or 240 mg twice daily × 4-8 weeks
medicines.use_case: As standalone mucosal protectant in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease (in addition to H. pylori eradication use); black stools — reassure patients

categories.category_name: Vitamin B12 Replacement — Autoimmune Gastritis / Pernicious Anaemia
categories.purpose: Replacement of Vitamin B12 in autoimmune gastritis where intrinsic factor deficiency prevents oral B12 absorption from food. Critical for preventing and treating megaloblastic anaemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

medicines.name: Cyanocobalamin IM / Hydroxocobalamin IM
medicines.dosage: INITIAL (LOADING) DOSES for deficiency: Hydroxocobalamin 1000 mcg IM daily for 7 days (UK protocol); or 1000 mcg IM every other day for 2 weeks; then 1000 mcg IM every 3 months LIFELONG (autoimmune gastritis — intrinsic factor permanently absent); CYANOCOBALAMIN: 1000 mcg IM daily for 7 days loading; then 1000 mcg IM monthly (shorter tissue retention than hydroxocobalamin — requires more frequent injections)
medicines.use_case: PERNICIOUS ANAEMIA / AUTOIMMUNE GASTRITIS — MANDATORY LIFELONG REPLACEMENT: intrinsic factor permanently absent so oral food-B12 absorption is essentially zero; IM injection bypasses the need for intrinsic factor (absorbed passively in ileum at very high parenteral doses); hydroxocobalamin preferred over cyanocobalamin (longer tissue retention — 3 months vs monthly injections)
medicines.monitoring: Serum B12 at 3-6 months after starting; FBC improvement (reticulocytosis within 1 week; Hb normalisation within 6-8 weeks); neurological improvement (slower — may take months; some permanent neurological damage if treatment delayed beyond 6-12 months of symptoms)
medicines.neurological_urgency: NEUROLOGICAL SYMPTOMS (numbness, weakness, balance difficulty) from B12 deficiency require IMMEDIATE daily IM injections for at least 2 weeks — neurological damage is rapidly reversible early but becomes permanent if treatment is delayed; do NOT wait for laboratory confirmation if clinical suspicion is high
medicines.india_note: IM B12 injection widely available and inexpensive in India; administered by any nurse or doctor; patients on lifelong autoimmune gastritis B12 replacement require quarterly GP visits for injections

medicines.name: High-Dose Oral Cyanocobalamin (Alternative for Non-Neurological Deficiency)
medicines.use_case: Alternative to IM injection in patients without neurological symptoms and who prefer oral route; HIGH-DOSE oral B12 bypasses intrinsic factor (approximately 1% of orally administered cyanocobalamin is absorbed passively without intrinsic factor — at high doses like 1000-2000 mcg, enough is absorbed to maintain normal B12 levels); evidence shows equivalent efficacy to IM for non-neurological deficiency in some trials
medicines.note: NOT appropriate for patients with active neurological symptoms — IM injection gives faster and more reliable correction; adequate adherence essential (daily tablet vs quarterly injection)

categories.purpose: Correct nutritional deficiencies caused by gastritis — iron deficiency from H. pylori-related malabsorption, chronic mucosal blood loss, or achlorhydria; other nutritional deficiencies in atrophic gastritis.

medicines.name: Ferrous Sulphate (Oral Iron)
medicines.dosage: 200 mg (65 mg elemental iron) two to three times daily; take on empty stomach for maximum absorption; or with Vitamin C (ascorbic acid 250-500 mg) to enhance absorption
medicines.use_case: Iron deficiency anaemia from: H. pylori-related iron malabsorption (H. pylori competes for iron; reduces ascorbic acid in gastric juice; promotes hypochlorhydria impairing iron absorption); chronic mucosal blood loss from erosive gastritis; achlorhydria in autoimmune gastritis (acid required for ferric → ferrous conversion, the absorbable form)
medicines.note: Separate by minimum 4 hours from PPIs (PPIs raise pH reducing ferric to ferrous conversion — reduces iron absorption significantly); H. pylori eradication may normalise iron absorption and allow iron deficiency to resolve without long-term supplementation

medicines.name: Calcium and Vitamin D Supplementation
medicines.dosage: Calcium 1000-1500 mg/day (as calcium carbonate — require gastric acid for absorption; use calcium citrate in achlorhydric patients — absorbed pH-independently); Vitamin D3 1000-2000 IU daily
medicines.use_case: Atrophic gastritis with achlorhydria (autoimmune gastritis) — calcium carbonate requires acid for solubilisation and absorption; switch to CALCIUM CITRATE which is absorbed independently of gastric acid; osteoporosis prevention in autoimmune atrophic gastritis; long-term PPI users (PPIs reduce calcium absorption)

medicines.name: Folic Acid
medicines.dosage: 5 mg once daily orally × 4 months (for treatment); 400-800 mcg daily (maintenance)
medicines.use_case: Folate deficiency in atrophic gastritis (especially with B12 deficiency — always test and treat both; isolated folate replacement without B12 in pernicious anaemia can worsen neurological damage by allowing haematological improvement while neurological damage progresses — the 'masking' phenomenon); dietary folate supplementation

categories.purpose: Rapid short-term symptomatic relief of gastritis-related epigastric discomfort, heartburn, and nausea — not therapeutic for the underlying gastritis.

medicines.name: Aluminium Hydroxide + Magnesium Hydroxide
medicines.dosage: 10-20 mL or 2-4 tablets after meals and at bedtime as needed
medicines.use_case: Immediate symptomatic relief of epigastric burning in gastritis; acid neutralisation; useful while awaiting PPI effect or as rescue medication; Mucaine (with oxethazaine — local anaesthetic) particularly useful for oesophageal and gastric burning
medicines.note: Separate from other medications (including PPIs, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, iron, thyroid hormone) by minimum 2 hours — chelation reduces absorption of many drugs

medicines.name: Prednisolone (Oral Corticosteroids)
medicines.dosage: Eosinophilic gastritis: 20-40 mg/day × 4-8 weeks; taper by 5 mg every 2 weeks once in clinical remission; Autoimmune gastritis: corticosteroids are NOT indicated (atrophy is irreversible; immunosuppression does not reverse parietal cell loss); Granulomatous gastritis (sarcoidosis): 20-40 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Eosinophilic gastritis failing dietary elimination; granulomatous gastritis from sarcoidosis (after TB excluded); not appropriate for H. pylori, autoimmune, or chemical gastritis

medicines.name: Proton Pump Inhibitors (High-Dose) — Eosinophilic Gastritis
medicines.dosage: Omeprazole 40 mg or esomeprazole 40 mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: Eosinophilic gastritis with predominant acid-related symptoms; PPI-responsive eosinophilic oesophagitis often extends to gastritis; some patients with eosinophilic GI disorders respond to high-dose PPI therapy alone

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet does not cause gastritis in the pathological sense — H. pylori, NSAIDs, and autoimmune mechanisms are the true causes. However, specific dietary patterns significantly influence symptom severity, mucosal healing, gastric cancer risk, and the progression of atrophic gastritis along the Correa cascade. The goals of dietary management in gastritis are: (1) reduce symptoms by avoiding mucosal irritants; (2) support mucosal healing through anti-inflammatory and antioxidant-rich foods; (3) reduce gastric cancer risk through dietary cancer-protective strategies; (4) correct nutritional deficiencies from gastritis complications (B12, iron, calcium); (5) facilitate H. pylori eradication by optimising the gastric environment.

dietary_principles.small_frequent_meals: 5-6 small meals per day instead of 3 large meals — reduces gastric distension, minimises acid secretion spikes, and reduces post-meal discomfort; particularly important in atrophic gastritis with impaired gastric motility
dietary_principles.anti_inflammatory_diet: Mediterranean-style diet — high in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, olive oil, and fish; low in red and processed meat; associated with 30-40% lower gastric cancer risk in multiple large epidemiological studies
dietary_principles.salt_restriction: HIGH SALT INTAKE is one of the strongest dietary risk factors for gastric cancer progression from gastritis; salt directly damages gastric mucosa (hypertonic saline is directly cytotoxic to gastric epithelium), increases H. pylori density, and upregulates CagA virulence factor expression; target <5g salt per day (WHO recommendation); avoid preserved, pickled, and salted foods — particularly important in North Indian cooking where salt and pickles are heavily used

recommended_foods.category: Anti-Inflammatory and Gastric Cancer Protective Foods
recommended_foods.evidence: Strong epidemiological evidence: high fruit and vegetable consumption associated with 30-50% lower gastric cancer risk

items.food: Cruciferous vegetables — broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, kale, Brussels sprouts
items.benefit: Sulforaphane (from glucosinolates in broccoli sprouts) is the most-studied dietary anti-H. pylori compound — inhibits H. pylori growth; reduces urease activity; suppresses H. pylori-induced NF-κB inflammatory signalling; reduces gastric mucosal oxidative stress; broccoli sprout extracts shown to reduce H. pylori colonisation density in clinical trials (Yanaka et al.); anti-cancer isothiocyanates inhibit gastric carcinogenesis
items.frequency: 3-5 servings per week; lightly steamed for maximum sulforaphane preservation
items.india_note: Phool gobhi (cauliflower), patta gobhi (cabbage), broccoli, sarson (mustard greens) — all members of this family; widely available and affordable in Indian markets

items.benefit: Allicin and organosulphur compounds — direct anti-H. pylori bactericidal activity (allicin inhibits H. pylori urease and disrupts bacterial cell membranes); anti-carcinogenic (inhibits nitrosamine formation — nitrosamines are gastric carcinogens); epidemiological studies: high garlic consumption areas in China and Korea have lower gastric cancer rates; also reduces NF-κB-mediated inflammation; protective against NSAID-induced gastric damage
items.frequency: 2-3 raw or lightly cooked cloves daily; crush and allow 10 minutes rest before heating (activates alliinase enzyme)
items.note: Raw garlic is more potent than cooked — cooking reduces allicin content; however, even cooked garlic retains other beneficial organosulphur compounds
