items.benefit: Curcumin — inhibits H. pylori CagA-mediated oncogenic signalling (c-Met/AKT/MAPK pathway); inhibits NF-κB activation in H. pylori-infected gastric mucosa; reduces gastric mucosal IL-8 and MCP-1 (chemokines that drive neutrophilic gastritis); anti-proliferative in gastric cancer cell lines; anti-angiogenic; Phase II trials suggest curcumin may reduce H. pylori density (adjunct, not monotherapy); black pepper piperine increases curcumin bioavailability 20-fold
items.frequency: Daily in cooking; haldi doodh (turmeric golden milk) at bedtime

items.food: Berries — amla (Indian gooseberry), blueberries, strawberries, pomegranate
items.benefit: Amla: richest Vitamin C source (600-900 mg/100g); Vitamin C is a key anti-H. pylori dietary factor — reduces gastric mucosal oxidative stress from H. pylori-induced free radical generation; Vitamin C in gastric juice converts potentially carcinogenic nitrite to harmless nitric oxide; Vitamin C supplementation in H. pylori-infected patients reduces mucosal oxidative stress and may modestly slow progression; Polyphenols (ellagic acid, quercetin, anthocyanins) in berries: anti-H. pylori adhesion; anti-inflammatory; antioxidant
items.frequency: 1-3 amla daily; other berries 2-3 times weekly

items.benefit: Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG): inhibits H. pylori growth (bacteriostatic MIC concentration achievable in gastric juice with regular tea consumption); inhibits H. pylori adhesion to gastric epithelium; reduces H. pylori-induced NF-κB; anti-inflammatory; anti-proliferative against gastric cancer cells; epidemiological data: regular green tea consumption associated with lower gastric cancer risk in Japanese population studies
items.frequency: 2-3 cups of unsweetened green tea daily; avoid green tea EXTRACT supplements (paradoxically hepatotoxic)
items.caution: Avoid very hot green tea — hot beverages (>65°C) classified as Group 2A carcinogen (probable carcinogen) by IARC — let tea cool slightly before drinking

items.food: Cold-pressed olive oil and mustard oil
items.benefit: Oleocanthal in extra-virgin olive oil: ibuprofen-like COX inhibition (anti-inflammatory) and H. pylori inhibition in vitro; omega-3 fatty acids in mustard oil (alpha-linolenic acid): reduce gastric mucosal inflammation; epidemiological: Mediterranean diet (high olive oil) associated with lower gastric cancer and gastritis progression risk
items.frequency: Replace refined oils with cold-pressed mustard oil, olive oil, or rice bran oil for cooking

items.benefit: Post-H. pylori eradication: probiotics restore gut microbiota disrupted by antibiotics; reduce antibiotic-associated side effects; Lactobacillus (particularly L. reuteri, L. rhamnosus, L. casei) — reduce H. pylori colonisation density (weak competitive exclusion); reduce H. pylori-associated gastric inflammation; improve H. pylori eradication rates when co-administered with antibiotic triple therapy (meta-analyses show +10-15% eradication improvement); reduce eradication regimen side effects (particularly diarrhoea and nausea) by 50%
items.frequency: Daily during and after H. pylori eradication therapy; continue 4-6 weeks post-antibiotic completion

items.benefit: 6-Gingerol and shogaols: (1) Inhibit H. pylori urease (H. pylori's key virulence enzyme); (2) Anti-H. pylori adhesion — prevent H. pylori binding to gastric epithelial cell Lewis b antigen (BabA-Lewis b interaction is the primary adhesion mechanism); (3) Anti-inflammatory — COX-2 inhibition, NF-κB suppression; (4) Gastric motility stimulant (prokinetic — improves delayed gastric emptying from achlorhydric gastritis); (5) Antiemetic; some in vitro studies show 8-gingerol more potent anti-H. pylori than clarithromycin at achievable concentrations
items.preparation: Fresh ginger tea 2-3 times daily; add to cooking

items.food: Banana (particularly unripe green bananas and banana powder)
items.benefit: Stimulates mucus secretion in gastric mucosa (protective mucous layer thickening); anti-H. pylori flavonoids (leucocyanidin in unripe banana); pectin (soluble fibre); Vitamin C; 'banana factor' increases gastric mucosal thickness in experimental models; traditional remedy for gastritis with genuine mechanism
items.frequency: 1-2 ripe bananas daily; banana powder (100g/day unripe banana in traditional management of gastric ulcer)

items.benefit: Stimulates gastric mucus secretion; promotes gastric prostaglandin E2 synthesis (mucosal protective); anti-H. pylori urease inhibition; anti-ulcer activity (comparable to antacids in some small trials); DGL form removes glycyrrhizin (which causes hypertension — use ONLY deglycyrrhizinated form)
items.preparation: DGL chewable tablets (available as Caved-S or DGL supplements); chew before meals
items.caution: ALWAYS use DGL form; never use whole licorice root regularly (glycyrrhizin causes hypokalaemia and hypertension)

items.food: Aloe vera gel (inner leaf — not the outer latex)
items.benefit: Acemannan and aloe polysaccharides: anti-inflammatory; promotes gastric mucosal healing; anti-H. pylori activity in vitro (reduces H. pylori adhesion and urease); reduces gastric acid secretion mildly; an RCT by Yusuf et al. showed aloe vera syrup equivalent to omeprazole for symptom relief in GERD
items.preparation: 30 mL fresh inner gel juice diluted in water, twice daily before meals
items.caution: Only inner gel — outer layer contains aloin (harsh laxative); not in pregnancy

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: High-Salt and Salty Preserved Foods — MOST IMPORTANT CANCER RISK REDUCTION
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Salt is the strongest dietary risk factor for gastric cancer progression from atrophic gastritis; hypertonic saline directly damages gastric mucosal cells; increases H. pylori density; upregulates H. pylori CagA oncogene expression; promotes N-nitrosamine formation; in Japan and Korea — dramatic reduction in gastric cancer mortality followed drastic nationwide salt reduction policies
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.specific_foods: Pickles (achar) — especially commercial high-salt varieties; papads; salt-preserved fish; salted snacks; excessive soya sauce; monosodium glutamate (MSG) in restaurant food; processed and packaged foods with high salt content
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Target <5g salt per day (WHO recommendation); reduce achar and pickled food consumption; limit papads; use salt alternatives (lemon juice, herbs, spices for flavouring)

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Nitrates and nitrites in cured/processed meats are converted to carcinogenic N-nitrosamines in the stomach by bacterial nitrate reductases; N-nitrosamines are among the most potent gastric carcinogens; smoked meats contain polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs); regular consumption associated with 15-25% higher gastric cancer risk in large cohort studies
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.examples: Sausages, ham, salami, bacon; smoked fish; commercially pickled meats
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Avoid processed meats; limit red meat generally to 1-2 times per week

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: NSAIDs are the most important pharmacological cause of gastric mucosal injury; never take on an empty stomach; always take with food; add PPI if gastritis is pre-existing or if NSAID use is prolonged
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Take all NSAIDs and aspirin WITH FOOD and a large glass of water; switch to paracetamol for mild-moderate pain; if NSAIDs essential — add PPI co-prescription

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Ethanol at concentrations >20% directly disrupts the gastric mucosal barrier; inhibits prostaglandin synthesis; causes acute mucosal congestion and haemorrhage; chronic use promotes achlorhydria and gastric atrophy; synergistically worsens H. pylori gastritis severity and impairs H. pylori eradication
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Avoid all alcohol during active gastritis symptoms and H. pylori eradication treatment; moderate intake (≤1-2 units/day) may be acceptable in stable chronic gastritis

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Strong Tea and Coffee on an Empty Stomach
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Caffeine stimulates gastric acid secretion (parietal cell activation); strong tea on empty stomach causes direct gastric mucosal irritation; tannins in strong tea reduce iron absorption (relevant in anaemia from gastritis); coffee is paradoxically gastroprotective for liver disease but direct gastric irritant for individuals with gastritis
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Never drink strong black tea or coffee on an empty stomach; always have with food or after meals; switch to weak chai with ginger; limit to 2-3 cups per day

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Very Spicy Foods During Active Gastritis
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Capsaicin activates TRPV1 receptors in gastric mucosa causing pain, increased acid secretion, and worsening visceral hypersensitivity in symptomatic gastritis patients; with acclimatisation (regular consumption), TRPV1 tachyphylaxis develops; sudden removal of spices in accustomed patients paradoxically sensitises TRPV1
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Gradually reduce spice levels during symptomatic flares rather than sudden elimination; replace chilli heat with non-capsaicin flavouring (black pepper — piperine, which modestly inhibits H. pylori; ginger; cumin)

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Hot Foods and Beverages — Cancer Risk
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: IARC classifies beverages consumed very hot (>65°C) as a Group 2A (probable) carcinogen for oesophageal and gastric cancer; thermal damage to gastric mucosa; particularly relevant in chai (Indian tea) drunk very hot; traditional boiling hot rasam
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Allow hot beverages and food to cool to <65°C before consuming (wait 3-5 minutes); blow on soup and tea before eating

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: The traditional recommendation of 'drink milk for gastritis/ulcers' is OUTDATED and COUNTERPRODUCTIVE — milk buffers acid momentarily but the calcium and protein in milk subsequently STIMULATE gastric acid secretion (protein is a major acid secretagogue) causing a REBOUND ACID INCREASE worse than the initial level; the Milk-Alkali syndrome (hypercalcaemia, alkalosis, renal failure) from excessive milk and antacid use is a recognised complication
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Moderate milk consumption is fine; PLAIN YOGURT is safe and beneficial (probiotic); do NOT use large amounts of milk as primary antacid strategy

sample_meal_plan_gastritis.principle: Anti-inflammatory; low salt; high Vitamin C; probiotics; moderate fat; small frequent meals; avoid triggers
sample_meal_plan_gastritis.early_morning: Warm water with 1-2 fresh amla (Vitamin C) or amla juice; ginger tea (anti-H. pylori, anti-nausea)
sample_meal_plan_gastritis.breakfast: Plain moong dal chilla (mung bean pancake — low fat, easily digestible); OR oats with banana and a few walnuts; OR idli with thin sambar (light, fermented — probiotic); weak ginger-cardamom chai (not on empty stomach — wait 15-20 min after water)
sample_meal_plan_gastritis.mid_morning: Fresh papaya or guava (Vitamin C); 5-6 almonds; plain curd (probiotic)
sample_meal_plan_gastritis.lunch: Brown rice or 1-2 whole wheat rotis (low salt) + moong dal or masoor dal + sabzi (steamed broccoli, cauliflower, or lauki in minimal oil with turmeric and black pepper) + small fresh curd
sample_meal_plan_gastritis.afternoon: Green tea with a few biscuits; banana; 1-2 walnut halves
sample_meal_plan_gastritis.dinner: Moong khichdi (ginger added during cooking) with a teaspoon of ghee + steamed vegetable; or dal-roti; light, low-salt, low-fat; early dinner — by 7-8 PM
sample_meal_plan_gastritis.bedtime: Haldi doodh (warm turmeric milk with black pepper and a pinch of cinnamon); DGL licorice chewable if symptomatic
sample_meal_plan_gastritis.avoid_today: Commercial achar, papads, fried snacks, red meat, very hot beverages, NSAIDs without food

nsaid_and_medication_review.overview: NSAID and aspirin use is the second most important preventable cause of gastric mucosal injury after H. pylori. Every patient with gastritis must have a thorough medication review — NSAID use is frequently undisclosed because patients do not consider OTC pain relievers as 'medications'.
strategies: Ask specifically about OTC ibuprofen, diclofenac, and aspirin use — 'Do you take any pain tablets? Combiflam? Brufen? Any tablets for fever or pain?' (brand-specific questioning in India improves disclosure)
Switch to PARACETAMOL (acetaminophen) for pain management when possible — no direct gastric mucosal toxicity at standard doses
If NSAIDs are essential (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis) — co-prescribe a PPI (omeprazole 20 mg) and take NSAID with food always
Consider COX-2 selective NSAID (celecoxib) for patients at high gastric risk
Test and treat H. pylori before starting long-term NSAIDs — the combination of H. pylori + NSAID has multiplicative (not merely additive) ulcer risk

smoking_cessation.reason: Smoking significantly worsens H. pylori gastritis through multiple mechanisms: increases H. pylori density in the stomach; suppresses mucosal prostaglandin synthesis; reduces antral bicarbonate secretion; increases parietal cell mass and acid secretion; significantly reduces H. pylori eradication success rates (smokers require longer antibiotic courses and have higher eradication failure rates); increases gastric cancer risk by 1.5-2× independently; delays gastric mucosal healing
smoking_cessation.advice: Smoking cessation at any stage of gastritis significantly improves outcomes and reduces cancer risk; use combination NRT + behavioural support + varenicline

alcohol_reduction.reason: Alcohol directly damages gastric mucosa, worsens H. pylori gastritis severity, impairs mucosal healing, and reduces H. pylori eradication success; disulfiram-like reaction with metronidazole (H. pylori eradication component) — must maintain complete abstinence during H. pylori eradication treatment
alcohol_reduction.advice: Complete abstinence during H. pylori eradication treatment (metronidazole component); reduce or eliminate alcohol in active gastritis; maintain within recommended guidelines once mucosal healing confirmed

stress_management.reason: Psychological stress worsens gastritis symptoms through the gut-brain axis — activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis; increases gastric acid secretion via CRF; impairs mucosal blood flow; worsens visceral hypersensitivity; stress-induced sympathetic activation reduces mucosal prostaglandin synthesis; stress events are strongly associated with dyspepsia flares and H. pylori virulence upregulation
strategies: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) for functional gastric symptoms with stress component

Mindfulness meditation (10-20 minutes daily — reduces cortisol and CRF); yoga and pranayama (improves vagal tone — parasympathetic activation improves gastric mucosal blood flow); regular aerobic exercise

cancer_surveillance_monitoring_for_atrop.overview: Endoscopic surveillance is the cornerstone of gastric cancer prevention in patients with established atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia.
surveillance_schedule: After H. pylori eradication: endoscopy and Sydney protocol biopsies — baseline; then OLGA/OLGIM staging determines surveillance intervals
OLGA/OLGIM Stage 0-I: endoscopy not required at 3 years; reassure; lifestyle advice; optional endoscopy at 5 years or if symptoms change
OLGA/OLGIM Stage II: consider endoscopy every 5 years

OLGA/OLGIM Stage III-IV: MANDATORY endoscopy every 3 years — HIGH RISK; high-definition white light endoscopy with virtual chromoendoscopy (NBI — narrow band imaging; FICE; BLI) for enhanced mucosal detail; systematic 5-site Sydney biopsies
Gastric dysplasia: surveillance every 12 months (low-grade); immediate endoscopic resection (high-grade)
Autoimmune gastritis: gastroscopy with biopsies every 3-5 years (gastric cancer risk 1% per year; Type 1 NET surveillance)
cancer_surveillance_monitoring_for_atrop.india_specific: ESGE/BSG surveillance guidelines apply; Indian gastroenterology centres increasingly adopting OLGA staging; given very high H. pylori prevalence in India, population-based H. pylori screen-and-treat programmes are being discussed as gastric cancer prevention strategy

green_zone.criteria: No haematemesis or melaena; mild epigastric discomfort; identified causative agent (alcohol, NSAIDs); able to eat and drink; improving symptoms
green_zone.action: Remove causative agent immediately; OTC antacids (Gelusil, Digene) for symptom relief; PPI (omeprazole 20 mg OD) for 4-6 weeks if NSAID-induced; GP review if not improved in 2 weeks; H. pylori testing if not previously tested

red_zone.status: EMERGENCY — Upper GI Haemorrhage from Erosive Gastritis
red_zone.criteria: Haematemesis (vomiting blood); melaena (black tarry stools); haemodynamic instability (tachycardia, hypotension); syncope
red_zone.action: CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112); IV access ×2; IV fluid resuscitation; IV PPI (pantoprazole 80 mg bolus); urgent endoscopy within 24 hours; blood transfusion if Hb <80 g/L

chronic_gastritis_h_pylori.after_eradication: H. pylori test of cure (UBT or stool antigen) at 4+ weeks post-treatment; LFTs, FBC, B12, ferritin if nutritional deficiency suspected; endoscopy if alarm features or no symptom improvement; OLGA staging if atrophy/metaplasia found
chronic_gastritis_h_pylori.surveillance_ongoing: Per OLGA staging intervals as above; annual B12, iron studies in atrophic gastritis

autoimmune_gastritis.monitoring: Annual: B12 levels, FBC, serum ferritin, calcium, thyroid function (associated autoimmune disease); annual serum gastrin (rising dramatically suggests ECL hyperplasia); CgA (off PPIs); endoscopy + biopsies every 3-5 years; dietitian referral for calcium and B12 management

complications.complication: Peptic Ulcer Disease (Gastric or Duodenal Ulcer)
complications.description: The most direct complication of H. pylori chronic gastritis — H. pylori disrupts the acid-mucus barrier allowing acid to penetrate and create mucosal defects. H. pylori is responsible for 90% of duodenal ulcers and 75% of gastric ulcers. NSAIDs cause peptic ulcers through prostaglandin depletion.
complications.management: H. pylori eradication (heals 95% of DU without recurrence); PPI; stop NSAIDs; endoscopy to confirm healing of gastric ulcers

complications.description: Bleeding from gastric erosions, ulcers, or portal hypertensive gastropathy. Erosive gastritis bleeding is usually low-volume and self-limiting; peptic ulcer haemorrhage can be life-threatening.
complications.management: IV PPI; endoscopy with haemostasis; IV fluids; blood transfusion; surgery rarely needed

complications.complication: Chronic Atrophic Gastritis and Intestinal Metaplasia
complications.description: Progressive loss of gastric glands with replacement by intestinal-type epithelium — the preinvasive phase of the Correa cascade. Largely silent but associated with progressive malabsorption and significantly elevated gastric cancer risk (OLGA Stage III-IV: 50-60× relative risk).
complications.management: H. pylori eradication; OLGA staging; endoscopic surveillance; dietary cancer prevention; nutritional supplementation

complications.description: The most feared complication of chronic H. pylori gastritis — gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal type) arising from the Correa cascade. The third most common cause of cancer death globally. H. pylori is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen. In India: gastric cancer is the 5th most common cancer; particularly high in Gangetic belt and northeastern states.
complications.management: H. pylori eradication at any stage reduces cancer risk by ~50%; endoscopic resection (EMR/ESD) for early gastric cancer (T1a, T1b); surgical gastrectomy for advanced; chemotherapy (FLOT/FOLFOX regimens); targeted therapy (trastuzumab for HER2-positive)

complications.description: B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue arising in the setting of H. pylori gastritis. H. pylori antigenic stimulation drives chronic B-cell clonal proliferation; in early localised Stage I-II disease: H. pylori eradication alone achieves complete histological remission in 70-80% of cases without chemotherapy. One of the very few cancers treatable with antibiotics alone.
complications.management: H. pylori eradication is first-line treatment for Stage I-II MALT lymphoma — 70-80% achieve complete remission; regular endoscopic and biopsy surveillance post-eradication; radiation therapy or rituximab for cases not responding to H. pylori eradication

complications.complication: Pernicious Anaemia and B12 Deficiency Neurological Complications
complications.description: Autoimmune gastritis → loss of parietal cells → absence of intrinsic factor → B12 malabsorption → megaloblastic anaemia AND subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (SACD — demyelination of dorsal and lateral columns). SACD causes: progressive ascending weakness; loss of vibration sense and proprioception; ataxia; spastic paraparesis; cognitive decline. SACD is irreversible if B12 replacement is delayed beyond 6-12 months of neurological symptoms.
complications.management: Immediate IM B12 (hydroxocobalamin) 1000 mcg daily for 7 days if neurological symptoms; then 1000 mcg every 3 months lifelong; monitor neurological recovery

complications.description: Multiple mechanisms in gastritis: H. pylori reduces iron absorption (competes for iron, depletes ascorbic acid); achlorhydria in atrophic gastritis impairs ferric-to-ferrous conversion; chronic mucosal blood loss from erosive gastritis; post-H. pylori eradication iron absorption normalises significantly.
complications.management: Iron supplementation; H. pylori eradication (may resolve iron deficiency without ongoing supplementation); investigate for other sources of GI blood loss if deficiency is severe

complications.description: Multiple small (usually <1 cm) ECL-cell neuroendocrine tumours in the gastric body/fundus of patients with autoimmune gastritis — driven by chronic hypergastrinaemia stimulating ECL cell proliferation. Type 1 NETs are indolent and rarely metastasise.
complications.management: Endoscopic resection of tumours >1 cm; endoscopic surveillance every 1-2 years in autoimmune gastritis; antrectomy (removing gastrin-producing antrum) can reduce hypergastrinaemia and cause carcinoid regression; somatostatin analogues for unresectable cases

key_points: H. pylori gastritis has been present for longer in elderly — higher prevalence of atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, and gastric cancer; OLGA staging critical
Autoimmune gastritis more prevalent in elderly — screen with anti-parietal cell antibodies and annual B12/FBC
NSAID use most common in elderly — highest risk of NSAID gastropathy and peptic ulcer; NSAID use for osteoarthritis often unacknowledged; always add PPI
Polypharmacy — multiple drug-drug interactions with PPIs; excessive PPI use contributes to falls risk (hypomagnesaemia causes tetany; bone fracture risk)
Cognitive symptoms from B12 deficiency in elderly may be misattributed to dementia — always check B12 in any elderly patient with cognitive decline
Lower threshold for endoscopy — any new or changed symptoms in patient over 55 years = endoscopy
H. pylori eradication should be DEFERRED until after delivery — most antibiotics in H. pylori regimens (clarithromycin, tetracycline, metronidazole in first trimester) have pregnancy concerns
Gastritis symptoms (nausea, vomiting, epigastric discomfort) are extremely common in pregnancy from hormonal changes (progesterone, oestrogen) independent of true gastritis
PPIs are generally considered safe in pregnancy (Category B) — omeprazole and esomeprazole preferred based on largest dataset; use when benefits outweigh risk
Sucralfate is the safest mucosal protective agent in pregnancy

Antacids: calcium carbonate (Tums) — also provides calcium supplementation; magnesium hydroxide — safe; aluminium hydroxide — short-term OK; sodium bicarbonate (Eno) — high sodium, avoid in hypertensive pregnancies
Iron deficiency from H. pylori gastritis may worsen in pregnancy — oral iron + Vitamin C for absorption enhancement
India has 70-80% H. pylori seroprevalence — effectively a universal infection in adults acquired in childhood; most have had asymptomatic chronic gastritis for decades
Test-and-treat strategy: in Indian primary care, any patient with dyspepsia, gastric/duodenal ulcer, unexplained iron deficiency, or ITP should be tested for H. pylori using UBT or stool antigen test

ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE in Indian H. pylori: clarithromycin resistance 15-30%; metronidazole resistance 50-80%; fluoroquinolone resistance rising; bismuth quadruple therapy (BQT) is increasingly the preferred first-line in India given these resistance rates

COST: H. pylori eradication in India is highly affordable — generic PPI (Rs 3-5/tablet) + generic antibiotics total regimen costs Rs 500-1,500 for a 14-day course; accessible at all hospital pharmacies

Gangetic belt gastric cancer: UP, Bihar, West Bengal — test and treat H. pylori at any age; even asymptomatic H. pylori-infected individuals in high-risk areas should be offered eradication (cancer prevention rationale)

CMV (cytomegalovirus) gastritis: occurs in severely immunosuppressed patients (HIV with CD4 <50, post-transplant on heavy immunosuppression); presents with bleeding gastric ulcers; diagnosis by gastric biopsy (viral inclusions, CMV immunohistochemistry); treatment: IV ganciclovir 5 mg/kg twice daily × 21 days; maintenance with valganciclovir
Cryptosporidiosis, microsporidiosis — can cause gastritis in AIDS; treat underlying HIV with ART

H. pylori gastritis in HIV: eradication with standard regimens is appropriate but eradication rates are lower; CagA-positive strains cause more severe atrophy in HIV-infected individuals despite low CD4 counts (paradoxically less H. pylori gastric inflammation with very low CD4 — immune system needed for the inflammatory response)
Post-transplant immunosuppression: H. pylori must be eradicated before transplantation (reduces post-transplant gastric complications and CMV risk)

vaccinations_recommended.reason: A prophylactic H. pylori vaccine would prevent acquisition of H. pylori, preventing the entire Correa cascade (chronic gastritis → cancer) from initiating; WHO has identified H. pylori vaccination as a priority for gastric cancer prevention globally
vaccinations_recommended.india_relevance: Given 70-80% seroprevalence in India, an H. pylori vaccine could prevent a substantial proportion of India's gastric cancer burden; research ongoing

HAV + pre-existing chronic liver disease is particularly dangerous.
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: All patients with chronic gastritis; travellers to endemic areas; food handlers

vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: Annual vaccination for all patients with chronic gastritis or atrophic gastritis

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between gastritis and an ulcer? Are they the same thing?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Gastritis and peptic ulcer are related but distinct conditions. Gastritis refers to inflammation of the stomach lining (mucosa) — the innermost layer of the stomach. The inflammation may be superficial and the mucosa remains largely intact. A peptic ulcer (gastric or duodenal ulcer) is a deeper wound — a break in the lining that penetrates through the mucosa into the muscle layers below. Think of gastritis as diffuse redness and irritation of the stomach wallpaper, while a peptic ulcer is a specific hole or crater in that same wallpaper. Both are very commonly caused by H. pylori and NSAIDs. The symptoms overlap — epigastric pain, nausea, and dyspepsia — but ulcer pain tends to be more severe, more specifically localised, often wakes patients at night, and may be relieved by eating (duodenal ulcer) or worsened by eating (gastric ulcer). Gastritis is diagnosed by endoscopy and biopsy; ulcers are diagnosed by endoscopy with visible mucosal defect. Both require treatment — H. pylori eradication is the key for both in the majority of cases.

frequently_asked_questions.question: My endoscopy showed 'chronic gastritis with H. pylori' — what does this mean and what should I do?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: This is one of the most common endoscopy findings in India — because approximately 70-80% of Indians are infected with H. pylori, a bacterium that colonises the stomach and causes chronic inflammation. 'Chronic gastritis with H. pylori' means the stomach lining shows persistent inflammation driven by H. pylori infection. The most important thing to do is ERADICATE H. PYLORI with a 10-14 day course of antibiotics plus a stomach acid tablet (PPI). The standard treatment in India is the bismuth quadruple therapy: PPI (omeprazole or pantoprazole) twice daily + bismuth subcitrate 4 times daily + metronidazole 3-4 times daily + tetracycline 4 times daily for 14 days. After completing treatment — CONFIRM ERADICATION with a urea breath test (UBT) at least 4 weeks after finishing the antibiotics (and 2 weeks after stopping the PPI). Do NOT assume treatment worked without this test. Successful H. pylori eradication resolves the gastric inflammation, heals ulcers, and reduces gastric cancer risk by approximately 50%.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I have been taking an omeprazole (stomach acid tablet) every day for years. Do I need it? Can I stop?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: This is one of the most important medication questions in gastroenterology — because PPIs (proton pump inhibitors like omeprazole, pantoprazole, rabeprazole) are massively overprescribed in India. Many patients are on lifelong PPIs prescribed years ago without a clear documented reason. Long-term PPI use is not harmless — it can cause Vitamin B12 deficiency (leading to anaemia and nerve damage), magnesium deficiency, increased risk of C. difficile diarrhoea, reduced calcium absorption, and possibly renal problems with very long use. You should ask your doctor why you are on a PPI and whether there is still a reason. Common valid reasons: active peptic ulcer disease; GERD with confirmed oesophagitis; long-term NSAID use; H. pylori eradication treatment (short course). If there is no clear ongoing indication, a PPI 'holiday' or step-down can be tried. When stopping long-term PPIs — DO NOT STOP ABRUPTLY — taper over 2-4 weeks (reduce to every other day, then stop) to avoid rebound acid hypersecretion which can cause temporary worsening of heartburn and trick you into thinking you still need the PPI.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is autoimmune gastritis and pernicious anaemia? How is it treated?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Autoimmune gastritis is a condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks the stomach's acid-producing parietal cells — the same cells that produce intrinsic factor (a protein essential for absorbing Vitamin B12 from food). When parietal cells are destroyed: (1) The stomach can no longer produce acid (achlorhydria); (2) Intrinsic factor is absent, so Vitamin B12 from food cannot be absorbed — resulting in pernicious anaemia (a specific type of B12 deficiency anaemia). Autoimmune gastritis is more common in women, typically diagnosed after age 40, and is associated with other autoimmune conditions (hypothyroidism, type 1 diabetes, vitiligo). Treatment: Vitamin B12 injections (hydroxocobalamin — 1000 mcg into a muscle) must be given LIFELONG — every 3 months — because oral B12 cannot be absorbed without intrinsic factor. Without treatment, pernicious anaemia causes: severe fatigue, breathlessness, and eventually irreversible neurological damage (numbness, weakness, balance problems from spinal cord damage). Regular endoscopic surveillance every 3-5 years is needed because autoimmune gastritis carries a small risk of stomach cancer and a type of benign stomach tumour called a carcinoid. Anti-parietal cell antibodies and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies in blood tests confirm the diagnosis.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can food cure gastritis? Are there any home remedies that actually work?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: No food or home remedy can cure gastritis caused by H. pylori (the most common cause) or autoimmune gastritis — these require specific medical treatment (antibiotics or B12 injections respectively). However, several dietary choices have genuine scientific support for reducing gastritis symptoms, slowing disease progression, and potentially reducing cancer risk: SULFORAPHANE in broccoli and broccoli sprouts — laboratory and some clinical evidence of anti-H. pylori activity; GARLIC — allicin inhibits H. pylori urease and adhesion; GINGER — blocks H. pylori's binding to gastric epithelial cells; TURMERIC (with black pepper) — curcumin inhibits H. pylori inflammatory signalling; AMLA (Indian gooseberry) — very high Vitamin C which reduces gastric oxidative stress; PLAIN YOGURT — probiotics reduce H. pylori density and improve antibiotic side effects during eradication. The most evidence-based dietary change for REDUCING GASTRIC CANCER RISK (the most dangerous complication of chronic gastritis) is reducing salt intake — high salt significantly accelerates progression from gastritis to cancer. These dietary strategies are complementary to medical treatment, not replacements.

frequently_asked_questions.question: My biopsy report mentions 'intestinal metaplasia' — is this cancer? Should I be worried?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Intestinal metaplasia is NOT cancer — it is a precancerous change (a premalignant condition) meaning the normal stomach lining cells have been replaced by intestinal-type cells. This is like an early warning that the stomach has been under stress (from H. pylori infection, dietary factors, or inflammation) for a long time. Whether intestinal metaplasia is concerning depends on its EXTENT and TYPE: if it is limited to the antrum (lower part of the stomach) and is the 'complete' (Type I) variety — the risk is relatively low; if it involves both the antrum and body of the stomach (extensive) and is the 'incomplete' (Type II/III) variety — the risk of eventual cancer is higher and regular endoscopic surveillance is needed. The most important step is H. pylori eradication if H. pylori is still present — this reduces further progression. Most gastroenterologists recommend endoscopic surveillance every 3 years for patients with extensive intestinal metaplasia (OLGA Stage III-IV). Do not panic — the progression from intestinal metaplasia to cancer is very slow (10-20+ years) and regular surveillance catches any progression at an early, treatable stage.
